The applicants were represented by Mr M. Filorinali and Ms Y. Başara, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The case of Mr Aydoğan and Ms Özen was adjourned for 11 hearings between 10 September 1999 and 19 October 2001. During this time the court ordered the continued detention of the pair at the end of each hearing. In October 2001 the Istanbul State Security Court, after having examined the evidence in the case file, convicted them as charged and sentenced them to death. As to the other applicants, the court decided to defer the imposition of a final sentence, pursuant to Law no. 46, and deferred the final sentence until the next hearing, on 6 February 2002. The court granted leave to the applicants’ lawyer to complain about this situation to the prosecutor and Minister of Justice. On 8 April 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The decision indicates that their lawyer, despite having requested the court to hold a hearing, had failed to attend it. On 24 September 2002 Mr Aydoğan’s and Ms Özen's sentences were commuted to life imprisonment. No information was submitted by the parties as to further developments. The court refused them leave to appeal since the decision in their respect was not open to appeal. The other applicants, however, were refused the chance to appeal in this respect as their decision in this regard was also not open for appeal.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1994 by the European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 19178/91) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. The applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 May 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mrs Liddy, Mr Owen and Mr Pannick as well as replies to its questions. The applicant appealed to the Secretary of State for the Environment under section 174 (2) (a), (b), (g) and (h) TCPA (see paragraph 19 below) An inspector was appointed to conduct an inquiry and determine the appeal. He was a Principal Housing and Planning Inspector, a civil servant and a member of the salaried staff of the Department of the Environment. The application was brought by Mr John Bryan, a farmer and a contractor. Inspector rejected the appeal under grounds (a), (b), and (g) but allowed it under ground (h) to the extent that the compliance period should be extended from three to six months. He held, inter alia, as follows: “The appeal on ground (b) ... (12) What I need to decide in respect of this ground of appeal is whether, as a matter of fact and degree, the buildings could, from their appearance and layout, be considered to have been designed for the purposes of agriculture. (13) In my opinion, as originally constructed,. the buildings would have led any reasonable person to have concluded that he or she was looking at the start of a small new detached housing estate. The appeal on ground (a) fails. The appeal on grounds (b) and (g) also fail. The buildings lie in part of the green belt but outside the village policy area for Higher Whitley. The use of domestic-style eaves and gable barge boarding. to that view. The residential look of the ‘porch’ to No. 1 building. And the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food’s view about the uneconomic layout of both buildings as originally built all add to the impression that these buildings were not designed for agricultural purposes, albeit they have since been modified and adapted for such a use. The High Court dismissed the applicant's appeal against the inspector's decision. Mr Bryan wanted more time in order to erect a replacement or replacements before demolition. The inspector had ‘erred in law in applying the wrong test in deciding whether the buildings were permitted development under the provisions of the ... General Development Order’. The appeal was dismissed by the High Court on 8 March 1991, the judge, Mr Lionel Read, QC, finding inter alia as follows: “A principal argument on behalf of the applicant at the inquiry under [ground] (b) was that the erection of the two buildings was permitted development. ... In my judgment ... it cannot be said that the inspector failed to take into account the fact that the applicant might ... erect buildings of a broadly similar nature”. Inspector extended the applicant’s time for complying with the enforcement notice under ground (h). Whether the existence of these General Development Order rights provided sufficient reason for the inspector to grant planning permission for the buildings in fact erected was a matter for judgment - the inspector's judgment. The question whether the alterations proposed to a building were, as he evidently thought, a ‘matter of cosmetics’ and would not meet the main objections was entirely a matter of planning judgment for him. If they are, their effect on the green belt, the countryside and the conservation area is irrelevant to the exercise of that right. In the result, I find no error of law and I dismiss the application.

U.S. had nevertheless committed a grave error in the deceased’s treatment and had thus violated basic principles of the medical profession. The EAW was forwarded by the British authorities to the German Federal Office of Criminal Investigation. On 20 March 2009 the Witten District Court issued the penal order (file no. 49 Js 174/08) against U.S., as applied for by the prosecution authorities. By a decision of the same day, the District Court determined that the probation period for U.K. was two years starting from the date the penalty order became final. U.B. was granted access to the files in the proceedings under file no.49 Js174/08 on 14 April 2009. U. had been convicted by final decision of a German court for the offence underlying the extradition request and the sentence imposed upon him was currently in the process of being executed. His extradition would therefore be contrary to the ban on double jeopardy as reflected in section 9 (1) no. 1 of the Act on Cooperation in Criminal Matters. Hamm Higher Regional Court, endorsing the reasoning of the Hamm General Prosecution Authorities, declared U.’s extradition inadmissible on 14 May 2009. A meeting between the representatives of the Bochum prosecution authorities, the CPS and Cambridgeshire police took place at Eurojust in The Hague on 1 July 2009. The content of these discussions is confidential. Criminal investigations in the United Kingdom were discontinued. The Westphalia-Lippe Medical Association applied for the opening of disciplinary proceedings against U. for breach of his professional duties in connection with the incidents on 16 February 2008. The proceedings regarding U.’s fitness to practice medicine before the Arnsberg District Government were discontinued at the end of 2010. A decision dated 27 April 2011 of the competent Münster Administrative Court sitting in a special formation as disciplinary jurisdiction for the healthcare professions reprimanded U. under file no. 49 Js 174/08. U. committed himself to refrain from practising medicine abroad in the future. An Inquest into the circumstances of the incident was held by the Cambridgeshire Coroner from 14 January to 4 February 2010. The latter returned the verdict that the deceased had been unlawfully killed as a consequence of the inadequate treatment administered by U.D. Subsequent investigations and proceedings were instituted in the United Kingdom following Mr. Gray’s death. The applicants’ compensation claims were settled with respect to all three defendants by consent orders of December 2009, January and August 2010. In addition, in 2009 the applicants brought civil claims for damages for unlawful killing arising out of negligence with the High Court against U., TCN as well as Cam Bridgeshire PCT.

The divorce was decreed on that same day. The parents of the child who was taken from her mother were ordered to pay the costs. The mother was allowed to return to the home, but the father was not allowed to see the child again. The child was eventually returned to his mother. The parents were ordered by the court to pay back the money they had spent on the child's care, but were unable to do so. The judge ordered that the child be returned to her mother in the next two weeks. The father was ordered to return the child to the mother, who was not able to see him again until after the next court date. The boy was then allowed to visit his mother again, but he was kept from seeing her again until September. The child was to stay in the home for at least 15 months. The child's mother and father asked the court to allow the child to stay with them. The court agreed and the child remained with the family. The case was adjourned until after the child was two years old. It was decided that the child should stay with the parents. The boy was taken to a local hospital to be treated for depression. He was then taken to hospital again where he was treated for two weeks. He then moved to a new home where he remained with his parents until the age of three. The family decided to keep the child with them as long as possible. The decision was made to release the child on 12 July 2001. On 5 March 2002 the applicant requested that a court decision be given immediately. On 9 February 2002 the child’s curator informed the court that she would need another six weeks to prepare her submissions. On 28 June 2002 the court requested the Youth Office to report on the child's present life circumstances and on the discontinuation of therapy. On 6 January 2003 the District Court proposed that the parents should abstain from making use of access rights for one year and that contact should be carefully re-established afterwards. The applicant rejected this proposal and submitted that recent visiting contacts between herself and her daughter had developed in a more positive way. On 24 April 2003 the Pankow-Weissensee District Court, following a hearing attended by the applicant, decided that the child should remain with the foster family. The child’s curator ad litem lodged an appeal with the Berlin Court of Appeal (Kammergericht). She considered the measures taken by the District Court to be disproportionate. The child was placed with the foster family as a temporary measure. She considered that the child's persistent wish not to see her parents should be respected. The applicant was unable to accept that a parent-child relationship had developed between the child and her foster parents. It followed that parental authority had to be withdrawn from both parents and transferred to the Youth Office. Furthermore, visiting contacts between the girl and her parents were suspended for one year. The appeal was dismissed and the child was returned to her foster family. The Court of Appeal quashed the District Court’s decision, transferred sole parental authority to the child's father and granted the applicant visiting rights once per month for five and a half hours each. All parties heard in the proceedings had confirmed that the child found a sense of security and stability in the foster family, where she had been living for six and ahalf years. The child had consistently expressed the wish to live with the foster families as a full family member. The Court of appeal found that there were no reasons to suspend the applicant's access rights. It also stated the child was free to visit her mother at any other time if she wanted to. The applicant was ordered to contribute to the costs incurred by the accommodation of her daughter in the foster family from 25 June 1997 until 31 December 1998. She lodged a complaint against the Court of Appeal’s decision, in which she gave a full account of the proceedings before the civil courts and alleged that the impugned decision was disproportionate and violated her right to the enjoyment of her family life under Article 6 of the Basic Law. The Federal Constitutional Court, sitting as a panel of three judges, refused to admit the applicant's constitutional complaint for adjudication in October 2004. In September 2005 the Berlin-Brandenburg Administrative Court of appeal refused to grant the applicant leave to appeal.

train_texts: Case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair trial by virtue of the prosecution’s failure to disclose all material evidence in their possession. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 14 May 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The case was heard by a Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) within that Section. The decision of the Chamber was that the application was admissible and no hearing was required.

The applicant was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment. Nugent had been the applicant’s business partner. Runham and Gray were arrested in January 1988 and the applicant was arrested in February 1988. The two alleged co-conspirators, who according to the prosecution had, together with the applicant, paid for Nugent to be murdered, were acquitted. The applicant complained to the Police Complaints Authority (PCA) about Suffolk Constabulary's refusal to disclose material evidence. The PCA reported that it could not support any allegation of murder.

The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a fair trial by virtue of the prosecution’s failure to disclose all material evidence in their possession. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The applicant was convicted of the murder of Christopher Nugent and sentenced to life imprisonment at Norwich Crown Court in 1989. The case was heard by the Court of Justice on 14 May 2002, and declared admissible. Nugent was found guilty of conspiring with two others to commit fraud. The pair were paid to carry out the fraud in exchange for their silence. The case was settled out of court in 1989. The two men were sentenced to between two and four years in prison. They were released after serving their sentences. The conviction of the two men was later overturned on appeal. The men were found not to have committed any crime. They also did not have to pay back the money they had been paid to do so. The trial was adjourned while the men were awaiting further proceedings. The decision was made to dismiss the case on the grounds of lack of evidence. The jury decided not to pursue the case. The Government says evidence not disclosed at first instance fell into two categories. The first type of evidence derived from the Holmes computer system used by the police officers conducting the murder inquiry. The second category of evidence related to the parallel investigation into mortgage fraud by a number of people, including the applicant and Nugent. The Government submitted that, following the applicant’s conviction, and in the light of developments in the common-law duty of disclosure (see below), the prosecution reviewed their position and decided that the data stored on the computer system did amount to disclosable material. Some 4,000 actions had been disclosed, one of which was referred to by the applicant in support of his appeal. Document no. 580 subsequently came into the applicant’s possession. It is a letter, dated 12 April 1988, from a firm of solicitors acting for Gray addressed to Detective Chief Inspector Baldry of the Suffolk Constabulary, and reads as follows: “... Further to our several discussions concerning Mr Gray, you will of course be aware that I did visit him in Leicester Prison on 26 March. He has requested a transfer either to Brixton Prison or Wormwood Scrubs if this is at all possible” The appeal was heard on 28 and 29 March 1994. Non-disclosure of evidence at trial was one of the grounds of appeal to the Court of Appeal. Court of Appeal dismissed appeal on 29 March 1994. No miscarriage of justice had occurred. Nugent’s dishonesty was made perfectly plain to the jury. There was overwhelming evidence that the appellant initiated a plot against the victim Nugent. The money actually paid was in our view out of proportion to a plot simply to ‘duff up’ the victim. The applicant believed that an inducement was promised to Gray by the prosecuting authorities in exchange for his testifying against him. In addition to the above letter, he referred to the fact that his tariff of imprisonment (that is, the period to be served before review by the Parole Board) under the life sentence had been set at twenty-five years, but was subsequently reduced. The applicant also alleged that during a meeting with political party representatives, General K.T. had threatened their relative, and one of his colleagues. Şevket Epözdemir left his house to go to his office, which was nearby. When he failed to arrive the family became concerned and contacted the authorities. The first applicant went to the police station in Tatvan, where she asked the police officers to find her husband. Unbeknown to the first applicant the body of her husband had been found by soldiers in the vicinity of the nearby town of Güroymak, in a ditch. He was blindfolded and there was a gunshot wound on his face. The body was examined by two doctors, who noted the existence of widespread injuries on many parts of the face. Doctors established the cause of death as cerebrovascular haemorrhagic shock caused by the gunshot wound. and the body which, according to the doctors, had been caused by physical trauma. The applicants sent letters to the offices of the Van and Tatvan prosecutors and asked to be provided with information regarding the steps taken in the investigation over the course of the previous ten years. The Van prosecutor’s office decided that it had no jurisdiction ratione loci to investigate the incident and forwarded the applicants’ letter (mentioned in the preceding paragraph) to the prosecutor in Tatvan. The Tatvan prosecutor opened an investigation file into the killing and informed the Ministry of Justice. The Güroymak prosecutor took a decision of non-jurisdiction ratione materiae. On 10 January 1995 the applicants brought compensation proceedings against the Ministry of the Interior. In their petition the applicants argued that the perpetrators of the killing had not been found, despite the fact that more than one year had elapsed since the incident. The applicants also submitted that, because of the failure to find and punish the perpetrators, they had suffered immeasurable pain and stress. On 16 December 1997 the Van Administrative Court decided to award compensation to the applicants, in accordance with Article 125 of the Constitution (see paragraphs 32-34 below). It held that when carrying out their duties the public authorities had an obligation to take the necessary measures. The Ministry of the Interior appealed, arguing that it had not failed in that obligation because the reason for the killing and the identity of its perpetrators had not yet been established. The applicants lodged an appeal with the Supreme Administrative Court against the decision. In reaching its conclusion, the administrative court noted that the investigation into the killing was still ongoing and, in any event, the deceased had never sought protection from the State. It thus held that the public authorities had not acted in breach of their duties. It further held that, as the conditions of the “social risk doctrine” had not been satisfied, it was not possible to award compensation to the family on the basis of the State’s “absolute liability” The appeal lodged by the applicants was rejected by the Supreme Administrative Court on 17 April 2003. The applicants maintained that the authorities had failed to take the necessary steps to prevent the attack on their relative and to find the perpetrators. The Ministry was therefore responsible for the pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage arising from the failures on its part. The final decision was served on the applicants on 3 January 2006. The decision was made to uphold the death penalty against the perpetrators of the killing. The appeal was rejected and the decision was upheld on 14 November 2005. A request made by the applicant for the decision to be rectified was also rejected.

As they proceeded along the road, they heard a crash behind them and turned to see on the opposite side of the road the red police car pulling alongside a car (Pearse Jordan’s) and ramming it up onto the footpath.

The inquest was due to recommence on 1 December 1997. However, it was adjourned on 19 November 1997 by the Coroner. eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (‘the Convention’) by a Bulgarian national, Mr Georgiev Cvetan Rangelov. The applicant served his full prison sentence until 19 June 2003. Since then, he was remanded in preventive detention. The application is now at the end of its second phase and the applicant is free to leave prison. The case was heard by the Regional Court of Upper Bavaria on 21 August 2003. The decision of the regional court was upheld by the Regensburg Regional Court on 21 November 2003. The applicant’s counsel was subsequently granted access to the applicant's personal files at Straubing Prison. The Regional Court found that it was very likely that the applicant would reoffend if released. He had been convicted of burglary on numerous occasions and had reoffended shortly after having served long prison sentences. The applicant continuously refused critically to reflect on his offences and felt persecuted and wrongfully convicted by the German courts. He was not admitted to a social therapy in Erlangen Prison he had applied for in 2002. The conditions of his detention had also not been relaxed (Vollzugslockerungen). Both of these measures were important conditions for arriving at a prognosis that he was no longer dangerous to the public. The Nuremberg Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the Regional Court’s decision of 26 February 2004. The court considered that it was illegal to retain a convicted person in preventive detention for an indefinite period of time only as a consequence of his foreign nationality. The applicant, represented by counsel, lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court. He notably argued that his right to freedom as guaranteed by Article 2 § 2 of the Basic Law was violated because his preventive detention was disproportionate. He also claimed that the refusal to admit him to a social therapy due to his imminent expulsion discriminated him because of his Bulgarian nationality. It found that his complaint had no prospects of success. The Federal Constitutional Court confirmed that measures relaxing the conditions of detention were a decisive factor for the prognosis of a convicted person’s dangerousness. The applicant neither claimed to have applied for such measures in the course of his preventive detention nor to have been unlawfully refused such measures. The decisions of the criminal courts were also not based on the fact that until then, no such measures had been granted. The criminal courts had rightly pointed out that due to the applicant's persistent refusal to accept responsibility for his offences there were no suitable measures to prepare him adequately for his release. Subsequent developments in the case have led to a review of the applicant’S preventive detention order. The Regional Court considered that the applicant’s continued preventive detention was still proportionate. The court would have to decide at the next periodic review whether the applicant was to be released for reasons of proportionality, despite the fact that he had not previously been granted relaxations in the conditions of his detention and had not been considered as no longer posing a threat to the public. The applicant filed a complaint under the new Act, claiming compensation in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage. He complained that constitutional court proceedings that lasted four years, six months and one day were excessively long, even taking the position and function of the Federal Constitutional Court into account. The judge rapporteur conceded that the applicant’s submissions were sufficiently substantiated for his constitutional complaint to indeed have been dealt with earlier on the basis of the actual reasoning given. However, it became clear that the 2007 case did not pose a problem of retroactivity and therefore did not affect the outcome of the applicant's constitutional complaint. The Federal Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint under section 97a of the Federal Constitutional court Act. Unlike the ordinary courts, the capacity and structure of a Constitutional Court were laid down in the Constitution. The scope for adaptation and for the acceleration of proceedings was therefore limited. The court maintained that the twelve-month wait had not been excessive considering that the court had opted to rule on a similar case concerning the pension rights of surviving partners in a civil union (the 2007 case) before the applicant's case. A new judge rapporteur had stepped in at the end of his predecessor's term of office and had had to finish cases of higher priority than that of the applicant. The Act on Protracted Court Proceedings and Criminal Investigations was published in the Federal Law Gazette – Part I, 2011, pp. 2302 et seq. – on 2 December 2011 and entered into force the next day. It introduced general provisions instituting a remedy against any kind of protracted court proceedings. Section 1 applied to criminal and civil proceedings – for details see Taron v. Germany (dec.), no. 53126/07, §§ 19 et seq., 29 May 2012. Section 97b (1) A decision on compensation and reparation shall be rendered by the Federal Constitutional Court. Such compensation may be claimed therefor save in particular cases where reparation by other means, such as a finding that the length of proceedings was unreasonable, is sufficient. Complaint of undue delay is only admissible if complainant has previously objected to the length of the proceedings. Complaint must be lodged in writing and set out circumstances purported to establish the unreasonableness of the length. In the event of a tie the complaint of unduedelay shall be dismissed. The complaints panel shall render its decision without an oral hearing. Reasons need not be given. The decision is not subject to appeal.“In the case of terminated proceedings whose length might still become or had already become the subject of a complaint before that court, it was not necessary to raise a complaint of. undue delay prior to filing a complaint claiming compensation”

The applicant ran a company which operated 20 chemist shops. Following financial problems, the company went into liquidation in February 1987. The evidence against the applicant consisted of detailed oral admissions that he had allegedly made to the police concerning his involvement in the three offences. According to police he was questioned on three separate occasions and contemporaneous notes were taken of his statements. However, he had declined to sign them. His defence during the trial was to maintain that these statements were not made by him. The trial and appeal proceedings took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg. The only witnesses called by the defence during the trial were the two police officers who had arrested him. He protested his innocence pointing out that he had not denied his numerous misdeeds in the past. Leave to appeal against the sentence but not the conviction was granted by a single judge of the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on 5 February 1985. The reference was heard on 18 July 1986 and judgment delivered on the same date. The applicant argued that the verdict should be set aside as unsafe and unsatisfactory because of certain shortcomings in the prosecution case, in particular, that certain information had been withheld by the police. In fact two fingerprints had been found which later turned out to be those of the next door neighbour who was a regular visitor to the house. It was argued by the applicant that the police officer had told lies and that his veracity as regards the admission statements was thus called into question. The Court of Appeal examined other impugned shortcomings which it did not consider to cast any doubt on the verdict. It was of the opinion that, even if these matters had been investigated, it would have made no difference to the outcome. Although this is a matter which perhaps casts the police in a somewhat lazy or idle light, we do not think in the circumstances there was anything unsafe or unsatisfactory in the end about these convictions.”

The court found S.D. and I.A. guilty of ill-treatment during the performance of their duties under Article 245 of the former Criminal Code, and sentenced them to imprisonment, which was converted to a fine. For treatment to be qualified as torture under domestic law, the victims needed to have been charged with a particular crime, whereas in the present case the applicants had only been suspects and were later released without charge.

The European Commission requested the Observatoire géopolitique des drogues (OGD – Geopolitical Drugs Observatory) to prepare a report on drug production and trafficking. The Commission asked the Observatory for a revised version of the report, with the names of the drug traffickers deleted. The report contained twelve chapters with the following titles. It related how, over a period of ten years, there had been a tenfold increase in the area of land that had historically been used for cannabis production in the region of Er Rif. Current levels of production made ‘the sharif kingdom a serious contender for the title of the world’s leading exporter of cannabis’. It was published in a book sold by the OGD entitled Etat des drogues, drogue des Etats (“State of drugs, drugs of States”) and containing a chapter on Morocco. Le Monde published a report commissioned by the European Union in 1994. The King of Morocco asked for criminal proceedings to be instituted against Le Monde. Mr Colombani, the editor-in-chief, and Mr Incyan, the author of the article, were summoned to appear in the Paris Criminal Court on charges of insulting a foreign head of State. In a judgment of 5 July 1996, the Criminal Court found that the journalist had merely quoted extracts from what was undisputedly a reliable report, without distorting or misinterpreting it or making groundless attacks. It accepted that he had acted in good faith and acquitted both him and Mr Colombiaani. The Court of Appeal found that the journalist had not shown that he had “contacted any Moroccan dignitaries, officials, public authorities or services for an explanation for the failure to match words with deeds”. The applicants were therefore found guilty of insulting a foreign head of State and sentenced to fines of 5,000 French francs (FRF) each. They were ordered to pay King Hassan II, who had successfully applied to be joined as a civil party to the proceedings, FRF 1 in damages and FRF 10,000 pursuant to Article 475-1 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court of appeal also ordered Le Monde to make additional reparation in the form of a report publishing details of the convictions. The Court of Appeal found that the charge of duplicity had been repeated twice and that the insistence on drawing the reader’s attention to the King in person was tainted with malicious intent. The article portrayed Morocco as the world's leading hashish exporter and alleged direct responsibility on the part of the Moroccan government and members of the royal family. The charge that pernicious statements had been made to dramatic effect solely in order to preserve the country's image’ was found to be ‘pernicious’ and ‘unjust’. The Appeal Court ruled that the article had been written with ‘malicious intent’ in mind.

The applicant, who was living in the neighbouring village, was suspected of having participated in the so-called “Başbağlar Massacre’ The applicant and twenty other individuals were charged under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. On 18 February 1997 the İzmir State Security Court ordered his release pending trial. On 23 October 1997 the applicant was acquitted. On 12 February 1999 the applicant lodged a complaint. with the Bakırköy Assize Court against the Treasury, requesting 1.000,000,0000 Turkish liras (TRL) in respect of pecuniary damage. The applicant was unofficially working for a dairy merchant six months a year, collecting cheese from local farmers. In return he was paid TRL 100,000,0000 per month. The Bakırköy Assize Court found that the applicant’s unjustified detention on remand for 384 days qualified for compensation. The Court of Cassation quashed the decision on the ground that the defendant had not been notified of the applicant's claim. On 18 September 2002 the judge rapporteur heard the applicant who repeated his previous statements. The court awarded the applicant TRL 113,266,974 for pecuniary damage. The Bakırköy Assize Court refused the applicant’s claim for interest which was not covered by Law no. 466. The applicant appealed. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision with a minor amendment regarding the costs and expenses. On 5 October 2004 the applicant was paid TRL 2,113,266,9740 plus TRL 1,233,300,0000 in statutory interest, applied with effect from 21 October 2002. The decision was upheld by the Supreme Court on 21 October 2003. The case was settled in favour of the applicant on 8 November 2004. The application was settled at a cost of TRL 3.2 million.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 633/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Hamburg, Germany. On 25 July 2001 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 16 February 2002 the applicant and his accomplices were indicted before the Bielsko-Biała Regional Court. On 19 April 2005 the President of the Fourth Section Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was charged with being a member of an organised criminal group. He was convicted and sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. On 16 December 2004 the Katowice Court of Appeal partly allowed his appeal. The applicant was acquitted of the charges. The remaining part of the proceedings, which was remitted, is pending. The application is still pending at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) in Strasbourg, France. The appeal is on behalf of the applicant and his co-accused, and is being heard at the ECHR’s Strasbourg office. The case is on appeal at the European Court of human rights (ECH) in Paris, France, and the appeal is ongoing.

The trial began on 23 March 1998. Between 23 March and 13 July 1998 the Krakow Regional Court held 13 hearings. The applicant was sentenced to four years’ imprisonment. The Supreme Court quashed the first– and second‑instance judgments and remitted the case to the Kraków Regional Court. The applicant was placed in a separate cell with an area of 6.29 square metres. He received visits from his common law wife, his son, his sister and other members of the family. name: Bengt Hellborg
train_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. By a decision of 30 November 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court.

The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations.

The case originated in an application (no. 47473/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Akarp. He is the owner of a property known as “Humanisten 1” located in the city of Lund, in the south of Sweden. On the property there is a one-family house, which was built in 1934. The applicant inherited the property from his father, who died in 1991. The request for tentative approval was motivated by the father’s wish to build a house suited to his age, as he had difficulties in walking up and down the stairs of his current home. The application was rejected by the Building Committee of Lund on 13 June 1991. On 12 June 1991 the City Building Director adopted a new detailed development plan.

The application was brought by the applicant's father, who died in 1991. The request for tentative approval was motivated by the father’s wish to build a house suited to his age, as he had difficulties in walking up and down the stairs of his current home. According to the detailed development plan in force, only one main building was allowed on the existing property plot. The Building Committee decided to postpone its reply to the request until a new detailed development plans for the area had acquired legal force, but only until 13 June 1991. Subsequently, on 12 June 1991 the City Building Director (Stadsbyggnadsdirektören) adopted a newDetailed Development Plan for Lund.

The applicant inherited the property from his father, who died in 1991. His late father had applied on 13 June 1989 to the Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) of Lund for tentative approval (förhandsbesked) of a plan to divide Humanisten 1 and build a new one-family house. The application was motivated by the father’s wish to build a house suited to his age, as he had difficulties in walking up and down the stairs of his current home. The Building Committee decided to postpone its reply to the request until a new detailed development plan for the area had acquired legal force, but only until 13 June 1991.

The applicant applied for a building permit for a new one-family house. The Building Committee refused to give tentative approval for the project. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) of the County of Malmöhus. The Board agreed with the applicant and quashed the City Building Director’s decision to adopt the plan and the earlier refusal of a tentative approval. The Land Survey recommended that the property plan for Humanisten 1 be repealed at the beginning of March 1993. The proceedings were at a standstill until January 1997 (see section 4 below) It appears that the applicant submitted new plans on 16 November 1992.

In 1991 the City Building Director adopted a. detailed development plan for Humanisten 1 by which a division of the property was prohibited. The Building Committee, on 14 August 1991, informed the applicant that he could not expect to be granted a building permit for a new one-family house and therefore did not give tentative approval for the project. The applicant appealed against both decisions to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen, - hereinafter ‘the Board’) of the County of Malmöhus. On 15 April 1992 the Building Committee granted the applicant a tentative approval, referring to his father’s initial application (of June 1989) for tentative approval of a plan to divide the plot.

The applicant applied for a building permit to build a new one-family house. The Building Committee refused to give tentative approval for the project. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Board (länsstyrelsen) of the County of Malmöhus. On 12 March 1992 the Board agreed with the applicant and quashed the City Building Director’s decision to adopt the plan. The Land Survey recommended that the property plan for Humanisten 1 be repealed at the beginning of March 1993. It appears that those proceedings were at a standstill until January 1997 (see section 4 below), when the applicant submitted new plans.

The Government quashed the Board’s decision to repeal the property plan for Humanisten 1 in 1996. The decision was made to facilitate a division of the property enabling the applicant to construct a new house on the resulting new plot. The Government observe that the entire block has long been occupied by buildings in accordance with the city plan and plot divisions. The block has 10 plots, the sizes of which vary between approximately 750 m² and 1100 m². .... The Government find that the suitability of the intended change of the. property and the development conditions within the block ought to be examined through a new. detailed development plan for the area.

The Land Survey observed that the Building Committee had, with binding effect, made the assessment that the addition of a new one-family house would be consistent with the detailed development plan. Several of the applicant’s neighbours opposed the measure with reference to the special character of the neighbourhood. The owners of two neighbouring properties appealed against the decision to the Board, claiming that the neighbourhood was worthy of preservation due to its special character. The Board visited the area before deciding on 24 September 1993 to reject the appeal. The neighbours appealed to the Government, invoking the same grounds as before the Board. The applicant also submitted his observations. On 14 November 1996 the Government quashed the Board's decision to repeal the property plan for Humanisten 1.

In 1993 the Building Committee repealed the property plan for Humanisten 1. The owners of two neighbouring properties appealed against the decision to the Board, claiming that the neighbourhood was worthy of preservation due to its special character. The Board visited the area before deciding on 24 September 1993 to reject the appeal. The neighbours appealed to the Government, invoking the same grounds as before the Board. On 14 November 1996 the Government quashed the Board’s decision. “The Government find that the decision ... ought to be considered in its context, namely to make possible a division of the property with the intention of constructing one more family house.”

The applicant applied to the Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) for judicial review under the 1988 Act on the Judicial Review of Certain Administrative Decisions. The court, unanimously, found that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. “According to section 1, section 6, of the [1987 Act] land may only be used for development if it is, from a public interest point of view, suitable for its purpose. .... According to point 2 of the aforementioned provision, a detailed development plan becomes relevant when a new single building is to be constructed, the use of which will have significant influence on its surroundings”

The Court, unanimously, found that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. The court held: “According to section 1, section 6, of the [1987 Act] land may only be used for development if it is, from a public interest point of view, suitable for its purpose. .... Supreme Administrative Court found that the Government’s decision was not unlawful and confirmed it. Supreme Administrative Court: Land may only be used for development if it is, from a public interest point of view, suitable for its purpose. Court: Government's assessment that the suitability of the intended change of the property and the development conditions within the block Humanisten ought to be reviewed through a new detailed development plan for the area, is within the scope of jurisdiction of the authorities in planning matters. The applicant was given one month to submit additional written observations. The court held: “According to section 1 of the [ 1988 Act] the Supreme Administrative court must examine if the Government's decision in the case is contrary to any legal rule”

The Supreme Administrative Court of Sweden has upheld the decision of the County Administrative Board to quash the lower instances’ decisions regarding the property plan. The Court found that the public interest in protecting the cultural heritage of the neighbourhood outweighed the applicant’s private interest. A request by the applicant for re-opening of the case was refused by the Supreme Administrative court on 10 April 2002. The applicant made a further appeal to the Government, which was rejected on 23 June 2004. The appeal has since been referred back for a new consideration by the Office of the Town Architects. The hearing will take place again on 23 July 2013.

The Court of Appeal in Lund, Sweden, upholds a decision by the County Administrative Board to quash a building permit application. The Court found that the public interest in protecting the cultural heritage of the neighbourhood outweighed the applicant’s private interest. A request by the applicant for re-opening of the case was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court on 10 April 2002. The applicant made a further appeal to the Government, which was rejected on 23 June 2004. The appeal has now been referred back to the Building Committee for further consideration. The Building Committee, in June 1995, adopted an amended detailed development plan which effectively prohibited a division of the applicant’s property, and the construction of another building on it. Upon appeal, the Board quashed the decision on the ground that it should have been decided by the Municipal Council (kommunfullmäktige) of Lund. The applicant appealed against the decision to the Board, which found that the public interest in protecting the cultural heritage of the neighbourhood outweighed the applicant's private interest. A request by the applicant for re-opening of the case was refused by the Supreme Administrative Court on 10 April 2002.

The Board quashed the Building Committee’s 15 April 1992 decision on the grounds that the tentative approval was contrary to the existing property plan and detailed development plan. Although they ought to have been aware of the. tentative approval in connection with the property plan issue, the decision had been formally. served or notified to them only in March 1999. The applicant appealed against this decision to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Skåne. In two separate decisions of 17 December 2001, the Administrative Court of Appeal refused the applicant leave to appeal in each case. In February and March 2002 the applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court.

The Board quashed the Building Committee’s 15 April 1992 decision on the grounds that the tentative approval was contrary to the existing property plan and detailed development plan. The applicant appealed against this decision to the County Administrative Court. The latter granted him four extensions between 5 May and 23 August 2000 of the time-limits for specifying his appeal grounds. In two separate decisions of 17 December 2001, the Administrative Court of Appeal refused the applicant leave to appeal in each case. The Supreme Administrative Court granted the applicant numerous extensions until 29 August 2003. The case was decided on the basis that the Board had wrongly ruled that there was no longer a tentative approval binding on the building committee.

The Board quashed the Building Committee’s 15 April 1992 decision on the grounds that the tentative approval was contrary to the existing property plan and detailed development plan. The applicant obtained extensions of time-limits for filing his written submissions in April and May 1999, and in September he asked the court to give priority to the case. In two separate decisions of 17 December 2001, the Administrative Court of Appeal refused the applicant leave to appeal in each case. The Supreme Administrative Court granted him numerous extensions until 29 August 2003 of the time- limits for specifying his appeal grounds. The Court ruled that there no longer existed a tentative approval which was binding on the building Committee.

In separate proceedings in 1997, the applicant requested the District Court (tingsrätten) of Lund to declare that the Municipality of Lund was liable to pay him compensation for both actual and potential damage caused by its refusal to grant his request for a building permit. On 15 September 2004 the Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal in both cases. The District Court found that the Building Committee had disregarded a clear and unambiguous provision in the 1987 Act, i.e. Chapter 8 section 34, which stated that a permit should not be granted without an amendment to the property plan. The Municipality denied responsibility for the refusal.

The applicant requested the District Court (tingsrätten) of Lund to declare that the Municipality of Lund was liable to pay him compensation for both actual and potential damage caused by the refusal to grant his request for a building permit. The Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal in both cases. The District Court found that the Building Committee had disregarded a clear and unambiguous provision in the 1987 Act, i.e. Chapter 8 section 34, which stated that a permit was only granted if the desired measure was authorised by existing plans. The Municipality denied responsibility and said that the applicant was aware of the need to modify the property plan and ought to have understood that he would be able to build without an amendment.

In separate proceedings in 1997, the applicant requested the District Court (tingsrätten) of Lund to declare that the Municipality of Lund was liable to pay him compensation for both actual and potential damage. The District Court found that the Building Committee had disregarded a clear and unambiguous provision in the 1987 Act, i.e. Chapter 8 section 34. On 15 September 2004 the Supreme Administrative Court refused the applicant leave to appeal in both cases. The applicant has appealed against the decision and is still awaiting the outcome of the appeal. The judge concluded that the decision to refuse the applicant a building permit was erroneous and that the applicant should have been compensated for the damage caused.

In 2001 the applicant instituted civil proceedings against the Municipality requesting compensation in an amount of SEK 3,000,000 for the damage he had suffered due to the refusal to grant him the building permit. He claimed that this damage corresponded to the market value of the part of his property upon which he would have built the house. The Municipality contested the request. In a judgment of 4 March 2003, the District Court of Lund noted that it was improbable that he would be granted such a permit. However, even if he were to be granted a permit, the decision would most likely be quashed on appeal. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal. In December 2003, it found that the applicant had not been able to demonstrate that the consideration of his application for a tentative approval by the Building Committee was binding.

In 2001 the applicant instituted civil proceedings against the Municipality requesting compensation in an amount of SEK 3,000,000 for the damage he had suffered. He claimed that this damage corresponded to the market value of the part of his property upon which he would have built the house. The Municipality contested the request. In a judgment of 4 March 2003, the District Court of Lund noted that the proceedings relating to the building permit were still pending and that it was improbable that he would be granted such a permit. Even if he were to be granted a permit, the decision would most likely be quashed on appeal. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal.

In 2001 the applicant instituted civil proceedings against the Municipality requesting compensation in an amount of SEK 3,000,000 for the damage he had suffered due to the refusal to grant him the building permit. He claimed that this damage corresponded to the market value of the part of his property upon which he would have built the house. The Municipality contested the request. The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Court of Appeal. In a judgment of 19 December 2003, the Court Of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment of 4 March 2003. It found that the applicant had not been able to demonstrate that the consideration of his application for a tentative approval by the Building Committee was binding.

The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Supreme Court, which on 23 May 2005 refused the applicant leave to appeal. The applicant had been denied a definite right to divide and build a new house on his property. Nor had he demonstrated that the Municipality’s handling of his case had caused the damage for which he had claimed compensation. The Supreme Court ruled in favor of the applicant and upheld the decision to deny him appeal leave. The appeal was dismissed and the application was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 26 May 2005. The Court of Appeals ruled that the applicant was entitled to appeal against the decision. The application was rejected and the case was dismissed.

The applicant appealed against the judgment to the Supreme Court, which on 23 May 2005 refused the applicant leave to appeal. The Municipality of Lund, while blameworthy, had led to his being denied a definite right to divide and build a new house on his property. Road Traffic Regulations (Strassenverkehrs- Ordnung) read: “All road-users have a duty to conduct themselves in such a manner as not to harm or jeopardise others or inconvenience or annoy them more than may be inevitable in the circumstances’. By Regulation 49(1)(1) and 49(5), it is a “regulatory offence’ (Ordnungswidrigkeit) to contravene Regulations 1(2) and 5(1) to (3) Such an offence is punishable by a fine. The driver of the car was likewise fined.

The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled on the use of the death penalty in the case of murder. The death penalty is a capital crime under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) Act. A person can be executed for the murder of a person if he or she is sentenced to 20 years in prison. The maximum sentence for a death sentence is 20 years (i.e. 25 years for a first conviction). The maximum penalty for a second conviction is 15 years. The fine for a third conviction is five years. A fine of $250,000 is the maximum sentence. The penalty for second-degree murder can be 20 years. In this case the maximum fine is 25 years.

The applicants have an inalienable and indefinite right to the use of wood (Einforstungsrecht) from certain plots of land now owned by the Republic of Austria. In 1870 and 1876 the applicant's predecessors were granted the right to exchange their right to use the wood for ownership of the land. eval_texts: Two Polish nationals alleged they had been deprived of their liberty during an unlawful search of their apartment and that the police had used excessive and unjustified force towards them. They complained of a breach of Articles 3, 5 and 8 of the Convention. By a decision of 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The parties do not fully agree about the facts of the case, which may be summarised as follows. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The application was dismissed by the Court on 18 October 2008. The Court ruled that the application was not admissible as it was not part of a wider case. The applicant and her friend lived in the house with the owner’s permission. On 16 June 1997 the applicants requested to be examined by a forensic medicine specialist. It was established that the first applicant had two long bruises on his left arm, and other bruises on the palm of his hand. The second applicant had a blue mark on her bottom (13 by 9 cm) It was stated that these bruises could have been caused by the use of police truncheons. The police left the house and warned the students that some of them were in an illegal situation as they were not registered as inhabitants of the house, and threatened that they would be in trouble if they submitted a complaint. The applicants requested the Wrocław District Prosecutor to institute criminal proceedings against the police for abuse of authority. On 23 December 1997 the prosecutor refused to do so. The prosecutor considered that the police action had been justified. The police could have reasonably suspected that the unlocked car had been stolen, even though it had not been reported as such. The further developments had certainly come as a surprise to both the police and other persons involved in the incident. The applicant was most probably hit once. The owner of the car gave the police the keys and documents to the car. While he was being taken into custody by the police, he hit one of them in the face. Thereupon truncheons were used against him. After that, the intervention was terminated. The prosecutor concluded that the measures taken by the police had been proportionate to the situation. Given that D. S. had been behaving aggressively, direct force had been used against him, including the use of truncheons and handcuffs. It was finally noted that the accounts of the facts given by the persons present at the scene, other than the police, were highly divergent, making it impossible to establish the facts of the case. The first applicant appealed. He argued that the police brutality and aggression had been totally unjustified. The police had entered private property and effected a search of the house. The applicants had been hit as they had ignored the order to let D.S. go so that he could be taken to the car. D. S. argued that he was a law-abiding citizen, a student of two university faculties and a member of the Municipal Council of his town. He had not given any reason to be beaten, verbally insulted and humiliated just at the whim of the police. The police should not intervene in private property at night and hit, insult and humiliate people just because they looked, or lived, differently. The Wrocław Regional Prosecutor upheld the contested decision. He considered that the police had been justified in so far as they wanted to verify the identity of the owner of the car. A company was granted loans to construct a plant for the production of wood-powder fuel. The bank refused to pay the remaining 2 million SEK of the loan. However, the company was declared bankrupt on 7 September 1994. In 1995, the applicants and a company named Boket Konsult AB (hereinafter ‘Boket’) claimed compensation from the bank for the damage allegedly caused by the bank's initial refusal to pay a last instalment.

On 28 October 1992 the company concluded a contract with a municipal energy company, Drefviken Energi AB, concerning deliveries of wood-powder fuel. On 7 September 1994 it was declared bankrupt. The bank instituted proceedings against the first and second applicants, claiming their joint liability for 1.1 million SEK of the company's loan in accordance with the personal guarantees they had signed. They claimed that that refusal had violated the terms of the loan contract and, in any event, that the bank had incurred liability for damages due to negligence, since it had been negligent in its initial refusal to pay the last instalment. On 24 February 1995, in a different action, the applicants and a company named Boket Konsult AB claimed compensation from the bank in the amount of 37 million Swedish kronor.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The charges against the applicant included leading an organised criminal group, leading participation in several robberies and illegal possessing of firearms. The applicant was born in 1968 and is presently detained in the Koszalin Detention Centre. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The application was dismissed on the grounds that the case was too complex and there was a risk that the applicant might tamper with evidence. The applicant's detention was prolonged beyond the statutory time-limit of two years. The Court justified its decision with reference to the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences and the complexity of the case which concerned an organised criminal group. The court acknowledged that the period of the applicant’s detention had been long. However, it was justified by the importance of the. case and the severity of the possible penalty. The decision was upheld on appeal on 13 January 2004. The application for release was dismissed on 22 October 2003. On 16 April 2004 the court granted the application while noting the prolonged application of preliminary detention with respect to the applicant. The applicant’s numerous applications for release and his appeals against the decisions prolonging detention were to no avail. The trial court held 43 hearings during which it heard 86 witnesses and the depositions of 130 other witnesses were read at the hearings. On 21 July 2004 the Opole Regional Court gave judgment. The applicant was convicted as charged and sentenced to twelve years’ imprisonment. On 19 April 2005 the Wroclaw Court of Appeal partly dismissed the applicant‘s appeal and lowered the sentence against him to eleven years' imprisonment. It is not clear whether a cassation appeal had actually been lodged. It appears that the applicant appointed for the applicant a legal-aid lawyer with the purpose of lodging on his behalf a cassated appeal.

The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The Court heard addresses by Mr Jacot-Guillarmod and Mr Levi for the Government, by Mr Schermers for the Commission and by Mr Schönenberger and Mr Mäder for the applicant. Following the hearing and at the Court’s request, the Delegate produced the copy of a document. On 30 March 1990, pursuant to Rule 51, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court. Jutta Huber, a Swiss national, resides in Zürich. She admitted making a living from prostitution, but maintained that she knew Mr K. and Mr B. only by name and that she did not pass on to them any of her earnings. On concluding his examination, the District Attorney signed a detention order (Verhaftsverfügung) remanding the applicant in custody on grave suspicion of having given false evidence. Mrs Huber was released on 19 August 1983. The criminal proceedings in the Zü Richards District Court 14 October 1983 ended with the applicant's acquittal. The case was referred to the Public Prosecutor’s Office (Staatsanwaltschaft) of the Canton. District Attorney J. instituted proceedings before the Judge in Criminal Cases (Einzelrichter in Strafsachen) at the Zürich District Court (Bezirksgericht) The trial took place on 10 January 1985, after the indictment had been accepted (zugelassen) Mrs Huber was acquitted on the ground that she had never been validly summoned to appear as a witness (vorgeladen zur Zeugeneinvernahme), which made her testimony unlawful and inadmissible. On appeal, the Court of Appeal (Obergericht) of the Canton of Zü rich fined the applicant 4,000 Swiss francs for attempting to give false evidence. Mrs Huber was accused of knowing Mr K. and Mr B. in accordance with the system of mutual assistance in criminal matters. Zürich District Attorney also exercises judicial power within the meaning of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the Convention at the stage of the investigation. She complained, inter alia, that the same District Attorney had both ordered her detention on remand and drawn up the indictment. The Federal Court dismissed the appeal by a judgment of 24 November 1986, which was served on 18 December. The appeals lodged by Mrs Huber were: The appeal to the Court of Cassation of the Canton of Züich 17. On 22 August 1986 she lodged a public-law appeal with the Federal Court. The Zürich District Attorney qualifies as an ‘officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power’ within the meaning of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the Convention. The status and powers of District Attorneys were laid down in the Courts Act of 13 June 1976 (Gerichtsverfassungsgesetz, “GVG”) The District Attorney conducts the investigation except in those cases where it is entrusted to the Principal Public Prosecutor or a judge (Article 25 StPO) He may make a detention order (Verhaftsbefehl - Article 55 StPO), the grounds for which he must state. He has to hear an arrested suspect within 24 hours. The District Attorney is the prosecuting authority before the “Judge in Criminal Cases’ and before the District Courts in cases concerning petty offences and misdemeanours. For the higher cantonal courts (the Court of Appeal and the Assize Court - section 72 GVG), this function is performed by the Principal Public Prosecutor. The combination of the functions of investigation and prosecution has given rise to case-law - at cantonal and federal level - which has recently been confirmed. The Zürich case- law was confirmed in a judgment of 13 June 1988 (Ante Djukic geg geg) The District Attorney has the status of a party in the proceedings (Article 178 para. 1 StPO) The Cantonal Court of Cassation stated that the District Attorney of the Canton of Zürich exercises judicial power. The complaint is unfounded. What is decisive is whether at the time of the arrest the decision was taken by an official who satisfied the requirements of Article 5 para. 3 (art. 5-3) of the European Convention on Human Rights. This question has been answered in the affirmative by the eminent courts referred to above. This finding that the functions discharged by that officer are compatible with the provisions of the Convention cannot subsequently be called in question on the sole ground that, once the investigation has been completed, the District attorney assumes the role of prosecuting authority. The European Court held not to be decisive by the European Court in its judgment in the Schiesser case. In 1989, 108 District Attorneys in the Canton of Zürich dealt with 17,647 investigations, of which 20.3% resulted in an indictment, 33.8% in the case being discontinued, 42.2% in a punishment order and 3.7% in referral of the case to a higher court. The number of cases in which the District Attorney personally conducted the prosecution in court does not appear in the statistics, but according to the Government it is very low. The European Commission declared the application admissible on 9 July 1988. It expressed the opinion, by twelve votes to two, that there had been a violation of Article 5 para. 3 of the Convention. Government confirmed the submissions put forward in their memorial. In that document they had asked the Court to hold “that Switzerland [had] not violated the ... Convention ... on account of the circumstances which gave rise to Mrs Jutta Huber’s application’. text of the Commission's opinion and of the three separate opinions contained in the report is reproduced as an annex to this judgment. The Government's submissions to the Court can be found in the annex to the judgment, as well as in the final report of the European Court of Human Rights. The final report is available from the European Commission at www.ec.europa.org/human rights.

When he was released from prison in April 1994 he began trading in telephones. This was the source of the GBP 17,000 in his building society account. The judge observed: “It is for the prosecution to establish, of course, on a balance of probabilities that he has benefited from drug trafficking, that is received any payment or reward in connection with drug trafficking. Here there is no direct evidence of that.”

He denied owning any of the cars registered in his name, claiming variously that each had been purchased and sold on behalf of a friend or stolen without insurance. He alleged that his only realisable assets were some GBP 200 in a building society. account and the fittings of a garage rented from the local authority. The applicant filed a written statement in response, in which he denied having benefited from drug trafficking. He claimed that in 1990-91 he had been convicted of car theft and required to pay GBP 25,000 to the insurance company which had indemnified the victims. He explained that in 1990-91 he had been convicted of car theft and required to pay GBP 25,000 to the insurance company which had indemnified the victims. Mrs María Iglesias Gil and A.U.I. complained of a lack of diligence on the part of the judicial authorities in dealing with her complaint of child abduction. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr J. Thomas Mulet, of the Palma de Mallorca Bar. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. J. María Iglesias Gil, born in 1961, is the mother of A.U.I., who was born in 1995. On 1 February 1997 A.A.A., abducted his son during an access visit and left Spain with him. The first applicant lodged a criminal complaint with Vigo investigating judge no. 5 alleging child abduction. On 4 February 1997 the investigating judge made orders for a nationwide search to be made for the child’s immediate return to its mother. In a decision of 20 December 1996, the Vigo Family Court awarded the first applicant custody of the child and the father access. On 3 June 1994 the couple divorced. Their son was born on 7 December 1995.

After passing through France and Belgium, he travelled with the child by air to the United States. The first applicant lodged a criminal complaint with Vigo investigating judge no. 5 alleging child abduction and applied to be joined to the proceedings as a civil party. On 4 February 1997 the investigating judge made orders for a nationwide search to be made for A.M.A and for the child’s immediate return.

Convention: "Removal or the retention of a child is to be considered wrongful where it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body’s law of the State in which the child was habitually resident" Article 2: “Contracting States shall take all appropriate measures to secure within their territories the implementation of the objects of the Convention.” Article 6 “A Contracting State shall designate a Central Authority to discharge the duties which are imposed by the Convention upon such authorities. ...” “Central Authorities shall cooperate with each other and promote cooperation amongst the competent authorities in their respective States to secure the prompt return of children”

Article 1: "Contracting States shall take all appropriate measures to secure within their territories the implementation of the objects of the Convention" Article 2: "For this purpose they shall use the most expeditious procedures available.” Article 3: "The removal or the retention of a child is to be considered wrongful where: (a) it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under the law of the State’s law" Article 6: "A Contracting State shall designate a Central Authority to discharge the duties which are imposed by the Convention upon such authorities. ...”

“The removal or the retention of a child is to be considered wrongful where: (a) it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a person, an institution or any other body; and (b) at the time of removal or retention those rights were actually exercised, either jointly or alone.” Article 6 “A Contracting State shall designate a Central Authority to discharge the duties which are imposed by the Convention upon such authorities. ...” “Central Authorities shall cooperate with each other and promote cooperation amongst the competent authorities in their respective States to secure the prompt return of children and to achieve the other objects of this Convention”

Article 8: “Any person, institution or other body claiming that a child has been removed or retained in breach of custody rights may apply either to the Central Authority of the child’s habitual residence or to any other Contracting State for assistance.” Article 11: The judicial or administrative authorities of Contracting States shall act expeditiously in proceedings for the return of children. Article 12: If a child is wrongfully removed, a period of less than one year has elapsed from the date of the wrongful removal or retention, the authority concerned shall order the child forthwith. Article 13: A court is not bound to order a child's return if there is a grave risk that its return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm.

The Convention provides for the return of children who have been wrongfully removed or retained. It also provides for an expedited process to secure the safe return of the child. The Convention also provides that the person, institution or other body having the care of a child can apply for assistance in securing the child's return. It adds that there is a grave risk that his or her return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable situation. (2) appropriate action on a transfer of custody to avoid the unsettling the child in a way that is harmful; (3) in general, any other action it considers expedient to remove the child from danger or prevent it coming to harm. All such measures may be ordered in any civil or criminal proceedings ...”

Minors shall enjoy the rights afforded them by the Constitution and international treaties ratified by Spain, the law states. The measures and action contemplated by Article 158 of this Code may also be ordered by the court, on its own initiative or on the application of any interested party. The judicial or administrative authority may also refuse to order the return of the child if it finds that the child objects to being returned and has attained an age and degree of maturity at which it is appropriate to take account of its views. Spanish courts have refused to characterise a failure by a person with parental responsibility for a minor to return the child as false imprisonment or kidnapping. Under the case-law, a person guilty of such conduct may only be prosecuted for criminal contempt or extortion under Article 556 of the Criminal Code, for which the punishment is six months’ to one year’s imprisonment. A parent who, without any justification, abducts his or her minor child shall be liable on conviction to between two and four years’ imprisonment and shall forfeit parental responsibility. train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 3252/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time’ within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the convention. The application was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). It was decided that the application should be considered in its entirety. The Government was represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Minsitry of Foreign Affairs.

The applicant was arrested on suspicion of having been involved in drug trafficking as a member of an organised criminal group. His detention was repeatedly extended by several decisions of the Szczecin Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) and the Katowice Court of Appeal. In their decisions, the courts repeatedly relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged, the serious nature of the offences and the risk that he would obstruct the investigation. After 15 March 2006 the applicant’s detention was extended three more times and the measure has still not been lifted. The court also stressed the severity of the likely sentence.

The case of Faruk Kalaç was heard in the Supreme Administrative Court of the Armed Forces. The applicant was a group captain with the high command’s director of legal affairs. He was ordered to retire by the Supreme Military Council for breaches of discipline and scandalous conduct. The court ruled in 1991 that the council's decision was final and not subject to judicial review. In their dissenting opinion the three members of the minority referred to the principle of the independence of the judiciary enunciated in Article 139 of the Constitution. They expressed the view that security of tenure for both civilian and military judges should not be breached. The case was decided in favour of the applicant.
