In 1990 he was serving, with the rank of group captain, as the high command’s director of legal affairs. On 1 August 1990 the Supreme Military Council ordered the compulsory retirement of three officers and twenty-eight non-commissioned officers for breaches of discipline and scandalous conduct. In a judgment of 30 May 1991 the Supreme Administrative Court of the Armed Forces ruled by four votes to three that it did not have jurisdiction to entertain the application. In their dissenting opinion the three members of the minority referred to the principle of the independence of the judiciary enunciated in Article 139 of the Constitution.

Josef Felix Müller’s paintings aroused “repugnance and disgust’. One of the paintings contains no fewer than eight erect members. All the persons depicted are entirely naked and one of them is engaging simultaneously in various sexual practices with two other males and an animal. Even the animals’ tongues (especially in the smallest painting) are more suggestive, in shape and aspect, of erect male organs than of tongues. The court is likewise unconvinced by the appellants’ contention that the paintings are symbolical. What counts is their face value, their effect on the observer, not some abstraction utterly unconnected with the visible image or which glosses over it.

An author is aware of a publication’s obscenity when he knows it deals with sexual matters. Not much of the argument in the appeal was directed to the issues of intention or of awareness of obscenity, nor indeed could it have been. As the trial court pointed out, the defendants at the very least acted recklessly. Similar pictures by Josef Felix Müller had been exhibited in Basle in February 1982 and it had not occurred to anyone to regard them as being obscene. As to the “publication’ of obscene items, which was prohibited under Article 204 of the Criminal Code, this was a relative concept. It should be possible to show in an exhibition pictures which, if displayed in the market-place, would fall foul of Article 204.

The paintings in issue show an orgy of unnatural sexual practices (sodomy, bestiality, petting), which is crudely depicted in large format. They are liable grossly to offend the sense of sexual propriety of persons of ordinary sensitivity. The artistic licence relied on by the appellant cannot in any way alter that conclusion in the instant case. eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) and by the Government of the Swiss Confederation. It originated in an application (no. 10737/84) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by nine Swiss citizens on 22 July 1983. Both sought a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 (Art. 10) The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs. D. Bindschedler-Robert, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) and Mr. R. Ryssdal, the President. President Ryssdal, who had assumed the office of President of the Chamber, consulted - through the Deputy Registrar - the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicants on the need for a written procedure. In accordance with the orders made in consequence, the registry received: (a) the applicants’ memorial, written in German by leave of the President, on 1 June 1987; (b) the Government’s memorial, on 30 July. The President directed on 23 October 1987 that the oral proceedings should commence on 25 January 1988 (Rule 38). The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. There appeared before the Court: O. Jacot-Guillarmod, Head of the Department of International Affairs, Federal Department of Justice, Agent; Mr. P. Zappelli, Cantonal Judge, Canton of Fribourg, Mr. B. Münger, Counsel; H. Vandenberghe, Delegate; P. Rechsteiner, avocat. Josef Felix Müller, a painter born in 1955, lives in St. Gall. The other nine applicants are: Charles Descloux, art critic, born in 1939 and living in Fribourg. The artists were meant to make free use of the space allocated to them. Their works, which they created on the spot from early August 1981 onwards, were to have been removed when the exhibition ended on 18 October 1981. The exhibition, entitled “Fri-Art 81’, was held as part of the celebrations of the 500th anniversary of the Canton of FribOURg’s entry into the Swiss Confederation. Josef Felix Müller produced three large paintings entitled “Drei Nächte, drei Bilder’ (“Three Nights, Three Pictures’) They were on show when the exhibition began on 21 August 1981. On 4 September 1981, the day of the official opening, the principal public prosecutor of the Canton of Fribourg reported to the investigating judge that the paintings in question appeared to come within the provisions of Article 204 of the Criminal Code. According to the Government, the prosecutor had acted on an information laid by a man whose daughter, a minor, had reacted violently to the paintings on show. Some days earlier another visitor to the exhibition had apparently thrown down one of the paintings, trampled on it and crumpled it. The court said the law did not define obscenity for the purposes of Article 204 CC [Criminal Code] The overall impression is of persons giving free rein to licentiousness and even perversion. The subjects - sodomy, fellatio, bestiality, the erect penis - are obviously morally offensive to the vast majority of the population. The artistic merit of the three works exhibited in Fribourg is admittedly less obvious than is supposed by the witness Ammann, who nevertheless said the works were 'beautiful' The court said: “Not without misgivings, the court will not order the destruction of theThree works.” All the applicants appealed on points of law on 24 February 1982. They challenged the trial court’s interpretation as regards the obscenity of the relevant paintings. The Art and History Museum of the Canton of Fribourg meets the requirements for preventing any further breach of Article 204 of the Criminal Code. The three confiscated paintings will be deposited there. At most they might escape destruction despite their obscenuity.“In the recent past, and still today, the public's general views on morality and social mores, which vary at different times and in different places, have changed in a way which enables things to be seen more objectively and naturally”. The court found that Josef Felix Müller’s paintings aroused ‘repugnance and disgust’ ‘These are not works which, in treating a particular subject or scene, allude to sexual activity more or less discreetly' ‘They place it in the foreground, depicting it not in the embrace of man and woman but in vulgar images of sodomy, fellatio between males, bestiality, erect penises and masturbation’‘The court is likewise unconvinced by the appellants’ contention that the paintings are symbolical. What counts is their face value, their effect on the observer’ The three paintings in issue do not on that account cease to be obscene, as the trial court rightly held them to be. Similar pictures by Josef Felix Müller, moreover, had been exhibited in Basle in February 1982 and it had not occurred to anyone to regard them as being obscene. It should be possible to show in an exhibition pictures which, if they were displayed in the market-place, would fall foul of Article 204. People interested in the arts ought to have an opportunity to acquaint themselves with all the trends in contemporary art.“On 18 June 1982, the applicants lodged an application for a declaration of nullity (Nichtigkeitsbeschwerde) with the Federal Court. A series of robberies and burglaries took place in the Coventry area. The police considered that there were some nine persons involved in the commission of these offences, including the applicant and his three co-defendants. The Chief Constable for the West Midlands decided to carry out a covert operation (“Operation Brassica”) The operation was to be carried out by arresting the suspects in groups, on suspicion of having committed different offences, and detaining them together in a police cell which had been specially fitted with covert audio equipment. It was hoped that the suspects would discuss the reasons for their arrest and that their ensuing conversation would be incriminating. The tapes were ruled admissible on 13 March 2000.

He said: “A man in a police cell is entitled to privacy just as much as a man sitting at his fireside in his own home.” Judge said he would have to decide whether the intrusion to privacy was 'in accordance with the law' There is no breach of Article 5, he said, and Article 6 has to be borne in mind but requires no specific findings from me at this stage. The trial judge also said: "It can perhaps be argued that whilst he is in a cell he not only does not have to say anything but if in fact he is free of guilt there is nothing that he can say"

A man in a police cell is entitled to privacy just as much as a man sitting at his fireside in his own home. He is after all innocent until proved guilty and he is in a vulnerable situation. Any bugging of his cell to intrude on his private conversation with another person would, prima facie, amount to an invasion of his privacy. If, on the other hand, he is guilty then he does not deserve the same right of privacy as anyone else. The weight of his loss of privacy is another matter which I may take into account. The main point which I have to decide is as to whether or not the intrusion to privacy was 'in accordance with the law'

The applicant together with three others was convicted on 20 July 2000 of various robbery and firearms offences. He was sentenced to a total of 8 years' imprisonment. The applicant and his three co-defendants appealed to the Court of Appeal, submitting, inter alia, that the tapes should not have been admitted in evidence. Lord Woolf CJ gave the judgment of the court on 13 February 2002, dismissing the appeal. He ruled that there had been a violation of Article 8 because the surveillance was not conducted according to law. He said: “This is because of the lack of any legal structure to which the public have access authorising the infringement”

In 1984 the Home Office issued Guidelines for the Use of Police Surveillance Equipment. The applicant and his three co-defendants appealed to the Court of Appeal, submitting, inter alia, that the tapes should not have been admitted in evidence. Lord Woolf CJ gave the judgment of the Court. of Appeal on 13 February 2002, dismissing the appeal. He said there had been a violation of Article 8 because the surveillance was not conducted according to law. In the exercise of my discretion under section 78, I will allow the tapes to be used in evidence and will not ban them from being played at a future hearing. The. appeal can in serious cases such as this be very important and is not objectionable.

In 1984, the Home Office issued the Guidelines for the Use of Police Surveillance Equipment. The applicant and his three co-defendants appealed to the Court of Appeal, submitting, inter alia, that the tapes should not have been admitted in evidence. Lord Woolf CJ dismissed the appeal on 13 February 2002, dismissing the appeal. He ruled that there had been a violation of Article 8 because the surveillance was not conducted according to law. He said that the non-compliance with Article 8 does not, however, mean that police officers have unfettered power. The tapes were allowed to be used in evidence under section 78 of the Human Rights Act.

Court of Appeal rejects argument that the arrests were for a lawful purpose as well as to enable the surveillance to take place. Arguments that the admission of the tapes in evidence prevented the defendants from receiving a fair trial were also rejected. Lord Woolf CJ said: “51. the tape-recordings cannot be relied upon as evidence. ... It is the responsibility of the Government to provide remedies against this violation of Article 8’ [§§ 66-67] The European Court of Human Rights recognises that to insist on the exclusion of evidence could in itself result in a greater injustice to the public than the infringement of Article8 creates for the appellants.”

Court of Appeal rejects arguments that tapes prevented defendants from a fair trial. Court of Appeal: Arrests were for a lawful purpose and the appellants were not therefore unlawfully deprived of their liberty. Lord Woolf CJ said: “The fact that the police were operating in accordance with a strategy designed to obtain additional evidence by covert recording does not turn lawful arrests into unlawful arrests.” He added: ‘On the evidence there were proper grounds for the arrests and ignoring the fact that police were working to an overall plan, there was nothing improper about the purpose for which the arrests took place.’ The remedy does not have to be the exclusion of the evidence. The remedy can be the finding that there has been a breach of Article 8 or it can be an award of compensation.

The European Court of Human Rights recognises that to insist on the exclusion of evidence could in itself result in a greater injustice to the public than the infringement of Article 8 creates for the appellants. The argument that the admission of the tapes in evidence prevented the defendants from receiving a fair trial was also rejected. Lord Woolf CJ said: “51. the tape-recordings cannot be relied upon as evidence. ... It is the responsibility of the Government to provide remedies against this violation of Article8’ [§§ 66-67] The remedy can be the finding, which we have now made, that there has been a breach of Article eight or it can be an award of compensation.

The Court of Appeal certified a question for consideration by the House of Lords concerning use of evidence obtained by an arrest for the purpose of eavesdropping on the defendant. Lord Woolf CJ went on to adopt the conclusions reached in other cases that there was no unfairness in admitting such taped evidence where there was not suggestion that the confessions were oppressively obtained or other than wholly reliable. On 30 May 2002, leave to appeal to the House Of Lords was refused. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled that the tapes did not need to be used as evidence in the trial of a man charged with robbery. The trial judge may have been unduly rigorous in his approach.

The Court of Appeal refused to overturn the conviction in the case of a Coventry man who was accused of conspiracy to commit armed robbery. Lord Woolf CJ said it was not contrary to the spirit of PACE or the Codes for there to be covert taping of what is said in the cells. He said there was no unfairness in admitting such taped evidence where there was not suggestion that the confessions were oppressively obtained or other than wholly reliable. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court, but the appeal was rejected and the case referred to the House of Lords. The appeal was heard by the High Court on 30 May 2002, and the decision was made to uphold the conviction.

The Court of Appeal certified a question for consideration by the House of Lords concerning use of evidence obtained by an arrest for the purpose of eavesdropping on the defendant. Lord Woolf CJ said: “If there was no unfairness caused by the tapes being relied upon in evidence then there is no breach of Article 6” [§ 69] The appeal was dismissed on appeal on 30 May 2002, leave to appeal to the Houseof Lords was refused. The case was referred to the Court of Criminal Appeal for consideration in the case of David Evans, who was charged with two counts of conspiracy to commit armed robbery in Coventry. Mr Evans was found not guilty of the charges, and the case was dismissed. The Appeal Court said the trial judge may have been unduly rigorous in his approach.

The applicant complains that the covert recording of his conversations by the police infringed Articles 8 and 13 of the convention. On 20 January 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible, partly inadmissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The tapes formed the basis of the case against the applicant and his three co-defendants. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. Tapes were ruled admissible on 13 March 2000. The trial judge held a ‘voir dire’ on the admissibility of the tapes. Counsel for the applicant argued that the methods of obtaining the evidence violated Articles 5, 6 and 8 of the Convention. The tapes should therefore be excluded under section 78 or section 76 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE), the trial judge said. The Chief Constable acted throughout in good faith, the judge added. The case was heard at the Crown Court in London and the verdict was delivered at the Royal Courts of Justice in London. The jury was instructed to deliberate for 30 minutes before delivering its verdict. There is no statute which provides for lawful bugging of police cells. There are however numerous cases where it has been considered and adopted. In fairness, if bugging is done it should not be done haphazardly and certainly does not bestow on police officers unfettered power. It is to this end that, in 1984, the Home Office issued the Guidelines for the Use of Police Surveillance Equipment. As I have already said, these are merely guidelines, they are certainly not statutes. The actions of the police and the decision of the Chief Constable have to be considered together with all the other matters. On the basis of all those matters, I have to consider in which way I should exercise my discretion. The applicant together with three others was convicted on 20 July 2000 of various robbery and firearms offences. He was sentenced to a total of 8 years' imprisonment. The applicant and his three co-defendants appealed to the Court of Appeal, submitting, inter alia, that the tapes should not have been admitted in evidence. Lord Woolf CJ gave the judgment of the Court. of Appeal on 13 February 2002, dismissing the appeal. As regards the admissibility of the tapes in evidence, the. Court considered the alleged violations of the Convention. It decided that there had been a violation of Article 8 because the surveillance. was not conducted according to law. The argument that the admission of the tapes in evidence prevented the defendants from receiving a fair trial was also rejected. Lord Woolf CJ said: “The complaints of the appellants with regard to the decision of the judge are not to the relevance of the contents of the tape. They were clearly highly relevant. ... On the evidence there were proper grounds for the arrests and ignoring the fact that the police were working to an overall plan, there was nothing improper about the purpose for which the arrests took place. ... This was a situation where the police was responding reasonably and proportionately to a very serious threat to the safety of the public and law and order" Lord Woolf CJ said the surveillance was not directly in conflict with any provision of PACE or the Codes. The Court of Appeal certified a question for consideration by the House of Lords concerning use of evidence obtained by an arrest for the purpose of eavesdropping on the defendant. On 30 May 2002, leave to appeal to the House. of Lords was refused. The case was referred to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) for further legal advice. The ECHR said it was “disappointed” that the case had been referred to and asked that the matter should be referred back to the ECHR for further advice.

The applicant was born in 1977 and lives in Istanbul. On 28 June 2003 two police officers went to the Beşiktaş district of Istanbul following a complaint by a woman, and imposed an administrative fine on a taxi driver. Subsequently, the policemen and the taxi driver commenced a verbal dispute in the presence of the applicant. The applicant told the police officers that he would pay the fine on his friend’s behalf. The police officers then pushed the applicant to the ground, handcuffed him and began kicking and punching him. He was subsequently put in the police car. One of the officers closed the car door on the applicant's leg. According to a medical report issued following X-rays and an orthopaedic examination, his right leg was broken.

The Istanbul public prosecutor filed an indictment with the 1st Chamber of the Istanbul Criminal Court against the police officers, charging them with ill-treatment of the applicant. The applicant joined the proceedings as a civil party. The court found, in the light of the medical reports that it had obtained, plus the witness statements and the submissions of the accused and the applicant, that the officers had beaten the applicant and had closed the car door on his leg and had thus caused the injuries found on the applicant’s body on 28 and 29 June 2003. The accused police officers were sentenced to two months and fifteen days’ imprisonment. As domestic legislation did not provide for an appeal, this decision was final.

The applicants complained that the existence of closed-shop agreements in Denmark in their respective areas of employment had violated their right to freedom of association. The applications were allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 of the Rules of Court) In a decision of 25 November 2004, a Chamber of judges relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, none of the parties having objected. Third-party comments were received from the Danish Confederation of Trade Unions (Landsorganisationen – LO), which had been given leave by the President. The Court heard addresses by Mr Lego Andersen and Mr Taksøe-Jensen, as well as their replies to questions from judges. The first applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Århus, Denmark. In the spring of 1996 he did his national service. He applied for a job as a holiday relief worker in a company, FDB Distributionen (‘FDB’) The applicant was offered the job from 3 June until 10 August 1996 and informed that his terms of employment would be regulated by an agreement concluded between FDB and a trade union called SID. Instead of applying for membership at the time of his appointment he had applied for membership. Denmark's Free Trade Union (Danmarks Frie Fagforening) represented the applicant in the case. The High Court found for FDB, stating as follows: “The High Court finds it established that the applicant was aware that membership of SID was a condition for his employment in the company. Thus, since the applicant did not comply with this requirement the conditions for dismissing him are fulfilled in accordance with section 2, subsection (2), in conjunction with subsection (1), of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act.” The case asked whether the Act is at variance with Article 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, in the light of the interpretation this Article has been given by the European Court of Human Rights. The Supreme Court of Denmark (Højesteret) upheld the High Court's judgment on 8 June 1999. The High Court said the domestic courts should disregard section 2(2) of the Protection against Dismissal due to Association Membership Act. A decision abolishing or limiting the existing possibility of entering into closed-shop agreements will have far-reaching consequences for the Danish labour market. The starting-point must be taken from the Act of 1992 incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights, the Supreme Court said. Hueth Wilson was sentenced to life imprisonment for buggery of a young girl in 1977. The court had before it psychiatric evidence to the effect that he suffered from mental illness. His tariff period (the minimum period of detention satisfying the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at six years and expired in April 1989. His time in prison was characterised by periods of thought disorder, delusions and behavioural problems and the Secretary of State decided that he was in need of care and treatment in a secure hospital. In August 1989, he was made the subject of a transfer direction and a restriction order and transferred to Broadmoor Special Hospital. In April 1994, the first applicant was transferred to Bracton Clinic Regional Secure Unit. On 1 July 1996, his case for discharge was considered by the Mental Health Review Tribunal and he was discharged. In June 1993 the Secretary of State decided that the second applicant should be regarded as a ‘technical lifer’. On 6 July 1996 the MHR Tribunal found that they were not satisfied that he no longer required treatment in hospital for mental illness. His case was reviewed most recently on 13 June 2000 when the Tribunal again did not recommend discharge. The Court of Appeal reversed the High Court's decision in part on appeal in 1994. A hearing was subsequently held in the Audiencia Nacional, in the course of which the applicant denied the murder allegations and resisted extradition. In a decision (auto) of 22 February 1991 a section of the Criminal Division of the Audieria Nacion ordered Mr Scott’s detention pending trial. On 2 January 1991 the British Embassy in Madrid wrote to the Audiancia Nadir that the sentence actually served upon conviction for murder was not likely to be more than ten years. A decision was made to extradite Mr Scott to England in March 1991. Mr Scott was arrested in 1990 on suspicion of the murder of his father. He had been detained pending the outcome of his rape trial. In May 1991 Mr Scott wrote to the Audiencia Nacional that he was willing to be extradited in order to get medical treatment in the United Kingdom. On 24 June 1991 the public prosecutor recommended that the applicant be kept in detention pending his trial for rape unless he could be temporarily handed over to the UK authorities. The British Embassy in Madrid wrote on 6 March 1992 that, in the event of the applicant’s temporarily handing over, his re-extradition to Spain could not be guaranteed. On 17 March 1992, taking 23 March 1990 as the date of the beginning of the applicants’ detention for rape, he was arrested again. The Audiencia Nacional had previously heard the public prosecutor and the applicant, the former having submitted that, given the impossibility of temporarily handing the applicant over to the United Kingdom authorities, his extradition should not take place. The appeal was rejected after summary proceedings in a decision (auto) of 6 May 1993. On the merits the Constitutional Court stated that the applicant had been detained in the extradition proceedings on 23 March 1990, so that the decision of 17 March 1992 to extend detention for two more years as of that date was legally correct. The earlier period spent in prison by the applicant was unrelated to the new detention. On 6 December 1992, following a further application by Mr Scott, the Audiencias requested the investigating judge in Puerto de la Cruz to supply information as to whether the applicant could be extradited. A statement by the complainant confirmed Ms T’s original allegations. Ms T. had received prolonged psychiatric treatment after her return from Tenerife. The applicant was subsequently committed for trial. In a judgment of 21 March 1994 the Audiencia Provincial acquitted the applicant on the rape charge on the ground that the only evidence incriminating him was Ms T's statements, which contained many inconsistencies. With respect to the forgery offence the applicant was convicted and sentenced as charged. In March 1994 he was handed over to the United Kingdom authorities, pursuant to the international arrest warrant. He spent a total of two years, six months and twenty twenty years in jail. On 9 November 1995, following a trial at Birmingham Crown Court, Mr Scott was convicted of the murder of his father. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. Employer also argued that the timekeeping documents could not be relied on as they were unofficial copies. The applicants requested that the court take other evidence into account, including the defendant employer’s shift orders, which detailed who would work when and for how long, as well as reports from the Regional Labour Inspectorate. Court asked the expert to supplement his report with findings concerning the parties’ objections. The applicants worked 24 hours in the course of a twenty-four-hour shift. They were awarded overtime in part. The Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance judgment on 28 October 2008 and remitted the case on the following grounds: “It can be seen from the case file that during the summer months [the applicants] worked for 24 hours and subsequently rested for 24hours; and in the winter months they worked for24 hours and then rested for 48 hours”. The employer appealed, arguing that the presumption established in the case-law that a person could not work more than 14 hours should be applied to the facts of the dispute. The court agreed and awarded the applicants compensation for overtime. An expert report calculated the applicants’ daily working time as 14 hours, in line with the Court of Cassation’s presumption of fact. The calculation in the new report led to no overtime being found for the weeks in which the applicants had worked three days as the working time was less than the legal limit of forty-five hours. The applicants appealed against the decision and maintained that the fact that they had worked continuously for twenty-four hours had already been confirmed by the legal records of the Ministry of Labour. Although they had proven that fact, the judgment had been based on the presumption that working for more than 14 hours a day was physically impossible.

On 15 June 2000 the Senior Disciplinary Board at the ministry for Public Service and Sport partly dismissed the applicant's appeal. It reduced the fine to approximately EUR 1,600.

The Appeals Commission at the Ministry for Public Service and Sport dismissed the applicant's appeal without holding a hearing. The applicant's arguments concerned mainly the question of his guilt, which was the subject of the disciplinary proceedings. It was not clear whether the applicant had made one of the statements at issue. However, having regard to all other statements it confirmed the Federal Minister's finding that the applicant could no longer be trusted to perform managerial duties as head of the Institute.

In the meantime, on 31 March 2000, the Federal Minister for Work, Health and Social Affairs recalled the applicant from his post with immediate effect (Abberufung mit sofortiger Wirkung) The Appeals Commission (Berufungs-kommission) at the Ministry for Public Service and Sport dismissed the applicant's appeal without holding a hearing. It noted that the authority deciding on the transfer did not necessarily need to wait for the outcome of pending disciplinary proceedings but could assess itself whether a civil servant had violated his professional duties and whether such a violation requested a transfer. There were, therefore, no reasons for his transfer.

In 1999 the Disciplinary Commission at the Ministry for Work, Health and Social Affairs found the applicant guilty of having violated his professional duties under the Non-Discrimination Act. It found that the applicant inter alia had made statements about some of his employees amounting to sexual harassment. On 15 June 2000 the Senior Disciplinary Board at the. The Appeals Commission dismissed the applicant's appeal without holding a hearing. On 6 December 2000 the applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof). He complained that the fact that the Appeals Commission had taken its decision after a private meeting was in violation of his right to court proceedings under Article 6 of the Convention. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint on 26 November 2001. It followed that Article 6 was not applicable to the applicant's case. It further found that there was no indication of arbitrariness in the proceedings at issue. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 13 February 2002. “Civil rights” within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention was not a matter of civil rights, it followed. It was not an issue of “civil rights’ or “the rights of others’” in the context of the case. There was also no indication that the proceedings were “arbitrariness’ in the circumstances’.

It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the Convention). The decision was made to deny the application the right to stay in prison while the application was heard. The appeal was dismissed and the case was dismissed.

In 2002 the applicant was held in a high-security prison which held Category A (high-risk) prisoners as well as Category B prisoners such as himself. While on bail pending trial, the applicant suffered a brain haemorrhage for which he underwent surgery. He expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence with his external medical specialist being read and applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters. All outgoing and incoming mail was to be marked ‘medical in confidence’ Outgoing correspondence would be checked to ensure that it was being sent to a nominated address. Incoming correspondence was to. be marked with a distinctive stamp of the relevant health authority. The latter would examine the content of the envelope in order to ascertain its medical content.

The applicant alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life under Article 8 of the convention. On 7 February 2008 the President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the treaty) The applicant wished to correspond confidentially with his external medical specialist to ensure that he would receive the treatment he needed. The applicant was concerned that his attempts to confirm that he was receiving adequate treatment in hospital might be regarded by the prison medical officer as criticism. He expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence with his external medical specialist being read and applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters. On 20 February 2004 the presiding High Court judge, Mr Justice Collins, allowed the applicant’s claim for judicial review. The judge concluded that there were exceptional circumstances in the applicant's case and his desire to ensure that his treatment in prison did not affect him adversely. The Court of Appeal concluded that although the procedure set out in the prison governor’s letter of 28 November 2002 amounted to an interference with the applicant's right to respect for his correspondence, the interference was justified and proportionate. Lord Justice Sedley gave the judgment of the court. It was noted that there was no dispute that the reading of prisoners’ correspondence was governed by law, and that it was directed to the prevention of crime and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. The issue to be decided was whether, in the language of Article 8 § 2 of the Convention, theReading of the applicant’S correspondence was proportionate to his Article 8 rights. The Court of Appeal concluded that the monitoring of the applicant’s medical correspondence was a proportionate interference with his Article 8 rights. It did not exclude the possibility that in another case it might be disproportionate to refuse confidentiality to medical correspondence in the prison context. The process by which the measure had been decided upon was not found to be arbitrary. In particular, it had not been the result of the rigid application of a policy. The withdrawal of monitoring had not only been considered but had been implemented until, upon reconsideration, monitoring had been resumed. It was recognised that there was an inescapable risk of abuse. However, the risk, having been minimised by virtue of confining surveillance to the prison medical officer, was outweighed by the above-mentioned factors. The applicant's current conditions of imprisonment are as follows: Category B prison in Staffordshire. Petition for leave to appeal was refused by the House of Lords on the ground that the petition did not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance. The application was rejected on the grounds that it was not of 'general public importance'

The appeal was quashed the contested judgment and remitted the case to the Bielski Regional Prosecutor, holding that a further investigation should be carried out. It considered that in order to assess the credibility of evidence given by the main prosecution witness, it was necessary to diagnose his personality and establish his perception skills.

The applicant’s lawyer informed the court that he had left for Greece in search of odd jobs and that he would be absent for some four months. In fact, the applicant returned after three weeks. In the circumstances, the court stayed the proceedings.

S.U. was indicted on the charges of homicide and uttering threats in 1995. The experts set the dates of the examination for 19 December 1995 and for 12 February 1996 respectively. However, S.u. did not keep his appointment for the examination on either of these dates. Eventually, he appeared before the experts on 9 May 1996 and was examined by them on that day. Their report was ready on 6 September 1996. On 30 December 1996 the Bielsko-Biała Regional Prosecutor lodged a new bill of indictment.

He was also absent at the hearing listed for 7 May 1999. In the circumstances, the court stayed the proceedings.

train_texts: The case was brought by an individual who claimed his right to a fair trial had been violated. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights, but no decision was reached. The court decided to hear the case again, and rule on the merits of the claim. The decision was returned to the Appeals Commission, and no further action was taken by the Court. The Supreme Court of the Republic of Austria ruled in favour of the applicant, and the case was thrown out. The matter was referred back to the Court of Arbitration for Human Rights for a new hearing, which was held on 18 February 2009. The Court of Appeal ruled that the application was not valid, and dismissed the case. The government appealed again, but the appeal was denied.

The case was brought before the Court of Appeal on 23 September 2009. It was decided not to rule on the merits of the case. The case was made under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention’s” Article 34). The decision to dismiss the case was based on the fact that there had been no hearing on the case prior to the appeal being heard. The decision was made to drop the case and the appeal was dismissed. The appeal was upheld by the Supreme Court on 24 September 2010. The Appeal was dismissed on 28 September 2010, and the case is now being appealed again.

He would also have to take decisions on questions of procedural and material law, give advice in difficult cases in his area of expertise (Fachgebiet), and represent the authority before the Independent Finance Panel (Unabhängiger Finanzsenat) The applicant was transferred to the post of specialist without any team-leading responsibilities.

The applicant appealed against the decision to the Appeals Commission on 18 May 2006. He argued, inter alia, that his actual work had not changed sufficiently to justify the lower grade. The Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint on 11 July 2007, finding that none of the legal provisions on which the contested decision had been based was in violation of the Austrian Constitution. The decision was served on the applicant's counsel on 21 August 2007. The application was dismissed on the basis that the applicant did not meet the legal requirements for justifying a transfer to another post.

On 23 September 2009 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Germany on 28 November 2010. The judge ruled in favour of the Austrian Government. The applicant was transferred to the post of specialist without any team-leading responsibilities. The job profile did not state that any employees or civil servants were to be under his direct supervision. The applicant complained to the Constitutional Court, arguing, inter alia, that the transfer had been arbitrary and violated his civil rights, as his salary had decreased in the new position. The Appeals Commission replied that the rights and obligations arising from employment in public service did not amount to civil rights and obligated to the applicant. The appeal was dismissed on 21 July 2006, and without holding an oral hearing, the Appeals Commission dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The European Court of Human Rights ruled in 2007 that the complaint was not in violation of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Strasbourg court ruled that there was no breach of the Convention and that the case could not be settled by an oral hearing. The European Court ruled in favour of the complaint on 11 July 2007. The case was heard by the European Court again on 21 August 2007 and the decision was upheld. The Court ruled that the original complaint had been made within the meaning of the Article 6 Convention, and therefore the case should not have been dismissed. The court issued a new ruling on 22 August 2007, saying that the application had been in breach of Article 6.

The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in Vienna. On 3 October 2000 the applicant was stopped by the police while driving his car on a public road. He was ordered to undergo a breathalyser test. After nine attempts to measure the amount of alcohol, among which only one was valid, the test was discontinued. The applicant appealed and argued that the DAA should have obtained the report of a technical expert on the functioning of the breathlyser. On 19 December 2005 the Lower Austria Regional Governor (Landeshauptmann) dismissed the applicant’s appeal. He found that according to the paper print out of the Breathalyser test the applicant had made four invalid attempts out of five. The DAA also ordered that an appeal had no suspensive effect.

The applicant was arrested by police officers for his alleged involvement in a fight and causing a disturbance while drunk. He was then taken to the police station inside the terminal building. The police officers allegedly covered the applicant’s head with his coat and started kicking, punching and beating him. They strangled him and banged his head against the wall. The applicant was released the next day without being brought before the public prosecutor. He then applied to the Human Rights Foundation of Turkey for the treatment of his injuries resulting from his ill-treatment in police custody. His symptoms included pain in the left side of the chest and back, and restricted movement of the left arm. The report noted that the symptoms were probably the result of physical trauma.

The Court considers it useful to outline the circumstances under which the parliamentary elections of 22 July 2007 took place. In early May 2007 the Turkish Parliament decided to hold early parliamentary elections. The decision followed a political crisis resulting from Parliament’s inability to elect a new President of the Republic to follow on from Ahmet Necdet Sezer before the expiry of his single seven-year term of office, on 16 May 2007. Fourteen political parties took part in the elections, which were marked by two characteristics. A strong mobilisation of the electorate was observed following the presidential crisis, since the participation rate rose to 84%. Secondly, political parties used two pre-electoral strategies to circumvent the national 10% threshold.

In the elections the AKP, the CHP and the MHP managed to get over the 10% threshold. The strong showing by independent candidates was one of the main features of the elections of 22 July 2007. There were none in the National Assembly in 1980 but 1999 saw them return, when there were three. In 2002 nine independent MPs were elected from a national total of 260 independent candidates. In 2007, twenty-seven independent MP were elected. More than twenty ‘thousand hopes’ candidates were elected, after obtaining approximately 2.23% of the votes cast, and joined the DTP after the elections. The independents also included a socialist MP, a nationalist MP and a centrist MP. In a Decree of 27 May 2007 the Higher Electoral Council (Yüksek Seçim Kurulu) said that it had chosen 25 June 2007 and 22 July 2007 respectively as the dates for the parliamentary elections in the polling stations set up at customs posts. The applicant lodged a request for the annulment of the Decree on 3 July 2007. But on 4 July 2007 the High Electoral Council dismissed the applicant’s request, on the basis of Article 94 II a) of Law no. 298. It pointed out that this provision could only be modified by a fresh legislative amendment. The application was dismissed.

The case was brought by a woman who wanted to keep her head covered. The case was heard by the European Court of Human Rights. The court ruled that the woman should be allowed to wear the headscarf. The woman was denied access to a lecture by the University of Bursa, where she worked. Her case was dismissed by the court on 11 December 2003, and she was not allowed to attend any lectures for the rest of the year. She was not given a reason for not attending the lectures, and was allowed to return to work the following week. The decision was made in accordance with the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), which states that it is the duty of the student to wear a head-covering. The applicant was refused admission to a neurology lecture and on 10 June 1998 to a written examination on public health for wearing a headscarf. She lodged an application for an order setting aside the circular of 23 February 1998. The Istanbul Administrative Court dismissed the application, holding that by virtue of section 13(b) of the Higher-Education Act (Law no. 2547 – see paragraph 50 below) a university vice chancellor, as the executive organ of the university, had power to regulate students’ dress. The Administrative Court held that neither the regulation in issue, nor the individual measures, could be considered illegal. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court, who dismissed her appeal on points of law. The applicant was suspended from Vienna University for a semester for taking part in an unauthorised assembly. The applicant appealed to the Istanbul Administrative Court to have the suspension quashed. On 28 June 2000 the applicant was granted an amnesty releasing her from all the disciplinary penalties and their effects. The Supreme Administrative Court held that the legislation made it unnecessary to examine the merits of the applicant’s appeal on points of law against the judgment of 30 November 1999. In the meantime, on 16 September 1999, the applicant had enrolled at Vienna University, where she pursued her university education. She has since completed her degree at the University of Vienna.

In October 1986, she underwent surgery to shorten her vocal chords. In August 1987, she was accepted on the waiting list for gender re-assignment surgery. Her treatment and surgery was provided for for her by the National Health Service. The applicant is a United Kingdom citizen born in 1937 and is a post-operative male to female transsexual. The applicant divorced from her former wife on a date unspecified but continued to enjoy the love and support of her children. The applicant claims that between 1990 and 1992 she was sexually harassed by colleagues at work. She attempted to pursue a case of sexual harassment in the Industrial Tribunal but claimed that she was unsuccessful because she was considered in law to be a man. She did not challenge this decision by appealing to the Employment Appeal Tribunal. She was subsequently dismissed from her employment for reasons connected with her health, but alleges that the real reason was that shewas a transsexual. Her record continues to state her sex as male and despite the “relevant domestic law and practice below” In a number of instances, the applicant stated that she has had to choose between revealing her birth certificate and foregoing certain advantages. She has not followed through a loan conditional upon life insurance, a re-mortgage offer and an entitlement to winter fuel allowance from the DSS. Nor did she feel able to report a theft of 200 pounds sterling to the police, for fear that the investigation would require her to reveal her identity. Similarly, she remains obliged to pay the higher motor insurance premiums applicable to men. The application was rejected by the Court of Appeal, which will decide whether or not the case should be returned to the High Court.

Three applicants were charged before the German courts with the commission of various criminal offences. Since they were not sufficiently familiar with the language of the country, they were assisted by an interpreter in accordance with German law. After conviction they were ordered, amongst other things, to pay the costs of the proceedings, including the interpretation costs. They consider that the inclusion of this latter item is contrary to, inter alia, Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention. They say that the use of interpreters should be limited to those who are not conversant with the German language. They argue that the obligation to employ an interpreter is, however, subject to one exception, namely when all the participants are familiar with a foreign language.

The costs of the proceedings are paid only after there has been a final ruling on the guilt of the accused. In the event of acquittal or of proceedings being discontinued, the Treasury in principle bears the costs. Article 6 para. 3 (e) (art. 6-3-e) of the Convention, which forms an integral part of the domestic law, specifies that “everyone charged with a criminal offence has the (right) ... to have the free assistance of an interpreter if he cannot understand or speak the language used in court“ This text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way.

The Code of Criminal Procedure states that the accused shall bear the costs of such part of the proceedings as concerned the act that gave rise to the conviction. This text has not been interpreted and applied by the German courts in a uniform way. Certain courts read it as embodying an obligation for the Treasury to bear costs in question for all time and in all cases. Other courts, including some higher courts, consider on the contrary that while Article 6 para. 3 (e) exempts an accused from paying in advance for the expenses incurred by the use of an interpreter, it does not prohibit such expenses being awarded against a convicted person.

The applicants appealed to the Court of Cassation against the judgment of the State Security Court. In their petition the applicants submitted arguments based on domestic law and challenged the veracity of their statements to the police. This decision was pronounced, in the absence of the applicants' representative, on 14 June 2000.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court on 18 July 1994 by the Government of the Kingdom of Spain (‘the Government’) and on 9 September 1994 by The European Commission of Human Rights. It originated in an application (no. 19382/92) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Netherlands national, Mr Antonius Adrianus van der Tang, on 2 December 1991. The applicant complained of the unreasonable length of pre-trial detention but who had absconded and evaded trial after being released on bail. The Court's object was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 3 ( art. 5-3) of the Convention. Antonius Adrianus van der Tang was arrested in May 1989. He was found driving a lorry which contained 1,300 kg of hashish. The lorry belonged to the applicant. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg on 20 February 1995. The Court heard addresses by the three of them as well as replies to its questions. The applicant was found in possession of a pistol with its serial number chiselled off and of a radio pre-tuned to a station which coincided with that of another set found. The Government's representative was given leave to address the Court in Spanish (Rule 27 para. 2) At least eight more people were detained for allegedly being involved in a three-stage operation to deliver about 7,000 kg of hashish. The applicant had only been driving for about ten minutes when he was arrested. Mr van der Tang made a written statement to Vigo investigating judge no. 1 in which he explained that, contrary to his previous statements, he had not known that he was transporting drugs at the time of his arrest. He had thought the consignment was tobacco but had said drugs because of the pressure put on him and language difficulties. An appeal by the applicant against this order appears to have been dismissed on 25 September 1989. Mr van der Tang lodged with investigating judge no. 1 his first applications for provisional release. Arguing that he had throughout been unaware of the real nature of the consignment, he insisted that he was not involved with any drug-trafficking organisation. He further complained that during his four-month detention he had only been questioned twice by the judge - in May and June 1989. The ground for the decision was the seriousness of the offences - illegal possession of a firearm and drug trafficking in large quantities. The second offence in itself attracting a prison sentence of “prisión menor en su grado medio’ (that is, from two years, four months and one day to four years and two months) Authorities had launched a nationwide operation (Operación Nécora) to combat a large-scale drug-trafficking organisation which operated mainly in Galicia. The applicant's case was transferred to Madrid on 29 October 1990. On 8 January 1991 central investigating judge no. 5 issued an order (auto de procesamiento) whereby new charges were added against the applicant without any alteration to the established facts. An appeal by the applicant against these orders which included a request for release was eventually rejected on 8 July 1991 by the Third Criminal Division of the Audiencia Nacional. The grounds for the decision not to release the applicant were the seriousness of the alleged offences, considerations of public order and the high risk of absconding. Van der Tang was arrested in 1989 and detained for two years. In January 1991 he renewed his application for release. His detention was extended by two years in May 1991. He was released on bail on 11 June 1992 on a condition that he paid a security of 8 million pesetas. The case was sent to the Third Criminal Division of the Audiencia Nacional for trial. Van der Tang has been in detention for more than three years. The application for bail was dismissed on the grounds that none of the issues raised by the applicant were of a constitutional nature. Mr van der Tang's subsequent constitutional complaint was declared inadmissible by the Constitutional Court on 11 September 1991. The period of time that has elapsed clearly owes much to ill fortune and the vicissitudes of the proceedings. He could have been tried in Galicia several months ago, when the Pontevedra public prosecutor did not oppose his provisional release. The accused has shown, at least to some extent, that he is able to remain on Spanish territory and obtain a contract of employment there which would enable him to engage in a lawful activity for the duration of the contract. The court did not consider that the accused's foreign nationality constituted an insurmountable obstacle to reaching this conclusion, because other foreign defendants in the case are in fact not being held in detention. On 23 December 1992 the applicant travelled to the Netherlands to spend Christmas with his family. His request was refused by the Audiencia Nacional on 24 November 1992 in view of the obvious risk of absconding. On 9 July 1993 the police informed the court that the applicant's whereabouts were unknown. He was ordered to appear before the trial court on 23 July 1993 at a hearing concerning the forfeiture of the bail. But the summons could not be served on him, as he no longer lived at the address he had originally given the Spanish authorities. By that time the case file ran to more than 22,000 pages. In respect of the applicant, the public prosecutor demanded a total prison sentence of fourteen years and a fine of 60 million pesetas. On 31 July 1993 the Audiencia Nacional, noting that the applicant had failed to comply with the conditions attached to his release, dismissed the objection and ordered his arrest. The trial took place in Madrid from 20 September 1993 to 24 May 1994. Mr van der Tang did not attend it and could therefore not be tried pursuant to section 841 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Luciano Núñez (see paragraph 8 above) was held to have played a leading role in importing very large quantities of hashish. He was accordingly sentenced to a total of thirteen years' imprisonment and a fine of 100 million pesetas.

The case of the Turkish Kurd in Switzerland. The case is based on the case of a woman who lost her hand in a car crash in 1987. The woman had been suffering from epilepsy. The father-in-law of the woman had applied for asylum. The judge ruled that it was not possible to prove that he was a victim of persecution. He was ordered to leave the country by 30 April 1989. The application was rejected on the grounds that he had not been able to prove his case. The family is still living in Switzerland and the woman is still in a care home. The man is now in his 40s and has a daughter.

The case was settled in 1988 and he returned to Switzerland, where he is still living. He is now waiting for a judge to rule on his application to be re-arrested and return to Turkey. It originated in an application (no. 23218/94) against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a Turkish national, Mr Riza Gül, on 31 December 1993. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 of the Convention. The Turkish Government, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not indicate any intention of so doing. Mr Gül is a Turkish national, who was born in 1947 and now lives with his wife at Pratteln in the canton of Basle Rural, Switzerland. On 25 April 1983 he travelled to Switzerland, where he applied for political asylum as a Kurd and former member of the Turkish Social Democratic Party (“the CHP”) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 October 1995. The Court heard addresses by Mr Danelius, Mr Plender and Mr Jacot-Guillarmod, and the latter’s reply to the question asked by one member of Court. In 1987 the applicant’s wife, who had remained in Turkey with their two sons, seriously burned herself during a fit brought on by her epilepsy, from which she had suffered since 1982. In December 1987, having found that it was impossible for her to obtain proper treatment in the area where she was then living, she joined her husband in Switzerland. Two of the fingers of her left hand were amputated. On 19 September 1988 in Switzerland Mrs Gül gave birth to her third child, Nursal, a daughter. As she still suffered from epilepsy, she could not take care of the baby, who was placed in a home in Switzerland, where she has remained ever since. Mr Gül applied for political asylum on humanitarian grounds in respect of himself, his wife and his daughter Nursal. The authorities took formal note of this on 8 November 1989. The final decision to grant a residence permit was given by the Federal Aliens Office on 15 February 1990. In a decision of 19 September 1990 the Aliens Police rejected Mr GüL’s request, on the ground that the conditions for family reunion had not been satisfied. The applicant appealed against this decision to the Basle Rural cantonal government (Regierungsrat) He argued that the residence permit issued to him and his wife under Article 13 (f) of the OLNA should have been extended to include his two sons. The Swiss government ruled that the boy was not entitled to the right to stay with his parents in Switzerland unless he had a permit. The decision was made on the basis of the Swiss constitution, which does not give parents the power to prevent their children from staying with them. The court ruled that there was enough room for the boy to stay if he was given permission to do so by the cantonal government. The boy’s parents were granted permission to stay as long as they were not allowed to leave Switzerland. They were allowed to return to Switzerland if they were able to prove that they could not leave the country without permission from the canton. According to the reference calculation, Mr Gül should have a monthly net income of at least 2,710 Swiss francs (CHF) if he is not to fall below the minimum standard of living. That figure is derived from the base rates used by the cantonal social security office for assessing the likelihood of reliance on social security. The cost of keeping the youngest child, Nursal, in a children’s home has not been taken into account, as it is not known who pays for this. The calculation of income is based on pay-slips from 1989, the latest available. On 23 October 1990 the Liestal Cantonal Hospital sent the Aliens Police the case. Basle Rural Aliens Police received a medical certificate stating that Mr Gül was 100% unfit for work and would remain so for a period that it was not possible to determine. For the first three months of this year alone the social security services have paid the family CHF 8,731.75, and the family will remain dependent on social security payments. For that reason alone the application for family reunion must be refused, writes the judge. The application must also be refused for the care of their other children, who will have to be brought up in a children’s home, the judge adds. If Ersin, 8, joined the family, it is not at all certain that firm arrangements could be made for his care. Ersin Gül has lived with Tuncay since birth. He has been separated from his father and mother for eight years and three and a half years respectively. The question arises, at the very least, whether it is reasonable to separate him from his brother and the environment he is used to in order to bring him to live with his mother, who is seriously ill and unable to keep him with her or look after him. In any case, there is no important reason within the meaning of Article 36 of the OLNA which requires him to be admitted to Switzerland.“ In view of all the circumstances, and having regard to the child’s welfare, the cantonal government considers that ErsinGül should not be authorised to join his parents in Switzerland. Mr Gül was granted a residence permit on humanitarian grounds to himself, his wife and his daughter. He lodged an administrative-law appeal with the Swiss Federal Court. The Federal Court found that neither section 17 (2) of the RSAA nor Article 8 (art. 8) conferred such a right on an alien resident outside Switzerland. In particular, Article 8 could be relied on only by a person who had the right of abode in Switzerland either by virtue of his Swiss nationality or by virtue. of a settlement permit, the court ruled. The court gave this ruling in the following terms: “Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights guarantees the right to respect for family life. According to the Federal Court’s established case-law, however, a breach can occur only where the family members living in Switzerland themselves possess a well-established right of abode (Anwesenheitsrecht). For that purpose, it is in principle necessary to have Swiss nationality or possess a settlement permit. A mere residence permit is at any rate not sufficient unless it is based on a firmly established right (see ATF 111 Ib 163/4 at 1a) ... That is, moreover, consistent with the new provisions on the legal status of aliens having family members in Switzerland (sections 7 and 17 (2) of the RSAA, as amended on 23 March 1990, which came into force on 1 January 1992) The applicant’s son Ersin has lived in Turkey since his birth, at first in Gümüsh. Several Courts of Appeal considered that the Court's findings in the case of M. v. Germany could not be applied at present by the domestic courts responsible for the execution of sentences. The Criminal Code as it stood did not permit its interpretation in compliance with Articles 5 and 7 of the Convention. It was therefore for the legislator to execute the court's judgment in the M.v. case. These Courts of appeal accordingly did not terminate the preventive detention of the persons concerned. Mr Tejedor García was an officer in the national police force and lived at Mataró (Barcelona) At about 8.30 p.m. on 21 May 1989, while off duty, he was in Gallur (Saragossa) where he joined members of his family and friends to celebrate his niece’s first communion. After a banquet which followed the ceremony and at which he drank, in addition to the wine that accompanied the meal, three glasses of champagne, a cognac and two half-measures of the wine, he drank. another bottle of wine. The facts underlying the procedure in issue were described in the judgment of the Saragossa Audiencia Provincial of 6 November 1991 (see paragraph 13 below) Manuel Tejedor García fired a shot into the ceiling of the café. He then kicked Mr Leonel Pajucides in the testicles after throwing the latter’s identity card to the floor saying that it was ‘shit’ Pointing his revolver at the two Africans, he forced them to leave the café with their hands above their heads and took them to the guardia civil barracks, where, finally, he handed them over to the officers on duty. These events provoked the indignation and disapproval of the people present who gathered round the police officer and his prisoners after following them from the café in Gallur. A preliminary inquiry was opened in respect of the applicant for wrongful arrest, assault and disobeying orders. The ANPU (Asociación Nacional de la Policía Uniformada) brought a private prosecution against the guardia civil officers of Gallur. It requested the court to declare that the applicant was innocent, and to investigate the responsibility of the two officers who had arrested him. On 10 September 1990 the investigating judge, having regard to the contradictory evidence as to the assault and the offer of drugs to the applicant, considered that no offence had been made out and decided, in accordance with Article 789 of the CCP (see paragraph 16 below) In an annotation of 7 November 1990 the registrar attested that the public prosecutor had returned the case file and lodged an application for the decision to be set aside. On the following day, the decision was served on Mr Gallego. In an order (providencia) of 8 November 1990, the investigating judge held that the application for an order setting aside the decision that no further action be taken had been made in the correct form. In a decision (auto) of 4 December 1990, a judge rejected MrGallego’s observations. The judge also ruled that the prosecutor had made the application in time, on the ground that it would be better to test the evidence at an adversarial hearing. On 12 February 1991 the investigating judge made a final discontinuance order (Articles 637 no. 2 and 790 no. 6 of the CCP) in respect of the two guardia civil officers accused by the ANPU. In the applicant’s case, he ordered an oral hearing and committed the applicant for trial in the Audiencia Provincial. The trial court noted that both the AN PU and the applicant were represented by Mr Gallego and requested him to clarify the situation. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal on 28 May 1993. The court said that the interpretation was not susceptible of constitutional relief. The appeal was rejected because it was not in line with the law, the court said. The applicant, Mr W. Weh, was born in 1952 and lives in Bregenz. He was fined 800 Austrian schillings (ATS) for exceeding the speed limit by 21 km/h. The trial is expected to be heard again in September. The defendant was sentenced to two years in prison, suspended for one year, with the possibility of a three-year extension if the case is re-heard by the Supreme Court again.

The case is described as an example of the use of the writ of habeas corpus by a Polish court to order the release of a man from a detention order. The verdict was overturned on appeal on July 6, 1998. The defendant was sentenced to a year in prison, to be served on a suspended sentence of two years, and to serve the rest of his sentence in jail. The sentence was suspended until the end of the case.

The judge ruled that he had been detained by a judge who was not authorised by law to detain him. The conviction was later overturned on appeal and the case was dismissed again. The defendant was released after three years on bail. The appeal was dismissed and the sentence was reduced to a fine of £1,000. It was the second in Poland, the third in Poland and the fourth in the EU. The sentence was upheld on appeal on 15 July 1998.

It found that the Civil Code, in choosing to regulate only two-parent adoptions, intended to treat the legal relationship between the adoptive parents and the adopted child as ‘a biological relationship’ The applicant appealed on points of law. On 15 March 2009, a new regulation entered into force entitled “Regulation on the implementation of mediation services for the adoption of minors” (“the Regulation”) enabling a single adoptive parent to have his or her forename registered in the place of that of the biological parent. The Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the court below.

While he was on the run from February 1997 until February 1999, he had had no sexual relations. The owner of the farm hostel gave evidence on the applicant's behalf. The most recent laboratory test, carried out on 18 March 1999, indicated that the applicant had a healthy liver. He had drunk approximately six strong beers a week and never got drunk. He dreamt of living on his own in a flat, supporting himself on sickness benefit. It was noted that subsequent to his return the applicant’s liver had returned to normal. The County Administrative Court delivered its judgment, finding against the applicant for the following reasons: “[The applicant] is HIV-positive and thus carries the HIV infection. He has been subjected to compulsory isolation since February 1995 and has during this period absconded from the hospital on several occasions – on the latest occasion for more than two years. During these two years he has used a false name and has been living a very secluded life, obviously owing to the risk of being discovered. A life at liberty makes great demands upon the person carrying the infection. During [the applicant's] contact with the doctors in question, they did not discuss the risk that he may spread the disease at all” The applicant again absconded, leaving his whereabouts unknown. He had appealed against the above judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal. He relied on an opinion of 14 May 1999 by the aforementioned chief physician and specialist in psychiatry, C.G., which stated that he was a man with a paranoid personality disorder, who misused alcohol. The Court finds that there is good reason to suppose that, if he remains free, [the applicant] will not comply with the practical instructions issued and that this entails a risk of the infection spreading. The diagnosis 'paranoid personality disorder' is defined as a pervading suspiciousness and lack of trust in other people, whose motives are consistently perceived as malicious. The applicant was diagnosed with the HIV virus in September 1994. He had been celibate since 1996 and had no longer any particular sexual desires or fantasies. He showed empathy as far as other people from those years were concerned. He was partly able to shoulder responsibility for his own mistakes, without blaming others. His attitude towards the county medical officer and the staff at the infection ward, whom he believed had kept harassing him unjustly, was almost hateful. He felt that he had been subjected to persecution between 1994 and 1995. This could possibly be interpreted as a symptom of delusion. From 1996, he had not experienced feelings of persecution, inter alia since he had secured his own liberty. He preferred sexual contact with boys around the age of 17. Several applications for an extension of the applicant's compulsory isolation were submitted by the county medical officer after June 1999 and granted. An application was turned down by the County Administrative Court on 12 December 2001. The applicant's whereabouts were unknown and that therefore no information was available regarding his behaviour, state of health and so on. It appears that since 2002 the applicant’s whereabouts have been known, but that there are no grounds for his further involuntary placement in isolation. His current location is unknown, but his condition is described as ‘stable’ and ‘good’ by the local medical officer. He was placed in isolation on 5 October 1999.
