The case originated in an application against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Commission on 21 September 1972. The purpose of the Commission’s request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 3 (art. 3) of the Convention. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir Gerald Fitzmaurice, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the convention) and Mr G. Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court. The Court heard the views of the Agent of the Government of the United Kingdom and the delegates of the Commission regarding the procedure to be followed. The oral hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 January 1978. There appeared before the Court: Mr. D.H. ANDERSON, Legal Counsellor, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr. L.J. BLOM-COoper, Q.C., Mr. J.W. Corrin, Attorney-General, Isle of Man, Counsel, Mrs. S.A. EVANS, Legal Advisers’ Branch, Home Office. Anthony Tyrer pleaded guilty in 1972 to unlawful assault occasioning actual bodily harm to a senior pupil at his school. He was sentenced on the same day to three strokes of the birch in accordance with the relevant legislation. The applicant was made to take down his trousers and underpants and bend over a table; he was held by two policemen whilst a third administered the punishment. The birching raised, but did not cut, the applicant’s skin and he was sore for about a week and a half afterwards. He appealed against sentence to the Staff of Government Division of the High Court of Justice of the Isle of Man. The appeal was heard and dismissed on the afternoon of 28 April 1972. The applicant was sentenced pursuant to section 56 (1) of the Petty Sessions and Summary Jurisdiction Act 1927. The sentence was governed by the following provisions: “(a) the instrument used shall, in the case of a child, be a cane, and in any other case shall be a birch rod.“ The expressions “child“ and “young person“ mean, respectively, an individual of or over the age of 10 and under 14 and an individuals of or under the ageof 14 and under 17. The instrument used in the sentence was a light cane of the following dimensions: Weight not exceeding 9 ounces Length from end of handle to tip of spray 40 inches. The whipping shall be inflicted on the posterior over the child’s ordinary cloth trousers. A medical practitioner shall be present during a birching and may at his discretion order the stopping of the punishment at any time. A report of the facts shall be forwarded immediately to His Excellency. In all cases where a Court is empowered to impose a sentence of whipping a medical report as to whether the offender is fit to receive the punishment will be made available to the Magistrates before they consider sentence. The Isle of Man is not a part of the United Kingdom but a dependency of the Crown with its own government, legislature and courts and its own administrative, fiscal and legal systems. Judicial corporal punishment of adults and juveniles was abolished in England, Wales and Scotland in 1948 and in Northern Ireland in 1968. The punishment remained in existence in the Isle of Man. In May 1977, by thirty-one votes for and only one against, Tynwald passed a resolution to retain the use of judicial corporalishment for violent crimes to the person committed by males under the age of 21. At the hearing on 17 January 1978, the Attorney-General for the Isle. of Man informed the Court that recently a privately organised petition in favour of the retention of judicial. corporal. punishment had obtained 31,000 signatures from amongst the approximate total of 45,000 persons entitled to vote on the Island. The name and address of a juvenile sentenced in the Isle of Man, whether to corporal punishment or otherwise, are not published. The average number of crimes of violence to the person per annum was: between 1966 and 1968 - 35; between 1969 and 1971 - 52; between 1972 and 1974 - 59; and between 1975 and 1977 - 56. In the three years 1975 to 1977, only one young male was convicted of a crime of violence. At the 1976 census, the Island’s population stood at 60,496. The applicant also claimed damages as well as repeal of the legislation concerned. The Commission, having considered ex officio that the facts of the case raised issues of discrimination on grounds of sex and gender, decided in favour of the applicant. The Commission decided not to proceed further with an examination of the original complaint under Article 14 (art. 14) which the applicant had subsequently withdrawn. The Commission decided that it could not accede to this request “since the case raised questions of a general character affecting the observance of the Convention’. The applicant took no further part in the proceedings. In its report of 14 December 1976, the Commission expressed the opinion that the judicial corporal punishment inflicted on the applicant was degrading and was in breach of Article 3 ( art. 3) of the convention. The report contains one separate opinion. The final decision was made on the application to the European Court of Human Rights.

The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10. The applicant association stated that it wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent it. On 23 April 1993, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members of the Chamber. The applicant association announced a series of showings, which would be accessible to the general public, of the film Das Liebeskonzil (“Council in Heaven’) The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 24 November. There appeared before the Court: Mr W. Okresek, Head of the International Affairs Division, Department of the Constitution, Agent, Mr C. Mayerhofer, Federal Ministry of Justice, Mr M. Schmidt, Advisers;. Mr P. Pellonpää, Delegate;. Professor F. Höpfel, Professor of Law at the University of Innsbruck, Counsel. The first of these showings was scheduled for 13 May 1985. All were to take place at 10.00 p.m. except for one matinée performance on 19 May. The charge was “disparaging religious doctrines’ (Herabwürdigung religiöser Lehren) The application was granted by the Innsbruck Regional Court (Landesgericht) the same day. As a result, the film was banned from being shown in cinemas in Tyrolean countries. The film was shown at a private session in the presence of a duty judge (Journalrichter) Public showings announced by OPI, the first of which had been scheduled for the next day, could not take place. Those who attended at the time set for the first showing were treated to a reading of the script and a discussion instead. As Mr Zingl had returned the film to the distributor, the “Czerny’ company in Vienna, it was in fact seized at the latter’s premises on 11 June 1985. An appeal by Mr Zedl against the seizure order, filed with the Innsbruck Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht), was dismissed on 30 July 1985. The film Das Liebeskonzil, in which God the Father is presented both in image and in text as a senile, impotent idiot, Christ as a cretin and Mary Mother of God as a wanton lady, came within the definition of the criminal offence of disparaging religious precepts. The court’s reasoning included the following: “The conditions of section 188 of the Penal Code are objectively fulfilled by this portrayal of the divine persons ...” The court ruled that the basic right of artistic freedom would in the instant case have to come second to the violation of legally protected interests. “Artistic freedom cannot be unlimited,” the court said. Mr Zingl appealed against the judgment of the Regional Court, submitting a declaration signed by some 350 persons who protested that they had been prevented from having free access to a work of art. The Innsbruck Court of Appeal declared the appeal inadmissible on 25 March 1987. The Attorney General decided on 26 July 1988 that there were no grounds for filing such a plea of nullity. The decision mentioned, inter alia, that the Attorney General’s Department (Generalprokuratur) had long held the view that artistic freedom was limited by other basic rights. There have been theatre performances of the original play in Austria since then. In Vienna the prosecuting authorities took no action. Oskar Panizza's play portrays God the Father as old, infirm and ineffective. Jesus Christ is portrayed as a “mummy’s boy’ of low intelligence. In 1895 Panizza was found guilty by the Munich Assize Court (Schwurgericht) of “crimes against religion’ and sentenced to a term of imprisonment. The play was banned in Germany although it continued in print elsewhere. The film, directed by Werner Schroeter, was released in 1981. It begins and ends with scenes purporting to be taken from the trial of Panizza in 1895. In between, it shows a performance of the play by the Teatro Belli in Rome. Film applauded the Devil. Film applauding the Devil is based on a. film applauding. the Devil by George C. Scott. The film applauds the Devil was released in the U.S. in the summer of 2013. The movie was directed by Tom Hanks and stars Hugh Jackman. It was released by Paramount Pictures, a division of Viacom, on September 28, 2013. It is directed by Hanks' son, John Hanks, and stars Robert De Niro, Michael Keaton, and David Carradine. It will be released in UK cinemas on September 23, 2013, and in North America on September 25, 2012.

The land was the object of land consolidation proceedings. The land owners claimed that they had not received adequate land in exchange for their land. They filed a complaint with the Administrative Court. On 15 December 1992, the Court rejected the complaint. The case was settled in favor of the owners of the land. The decision was made under Section 39 (2) no. 6 of the Land Reform Act of 1988. The application was dismissed on 5 July 1990, in the presence of the parties. The appeal was dismissed again on 5 September 1990, with the decision to be heard in public. It was decided that the appeal should be dismissed again in public, and the decision was upheld.

The case was first heard on 22 August 1984. In July 1989 the District Authority issued a consolidation plan. On 5 July 1990 the Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. In December 1992 the appeal was again dismissed. The case was finally decided on 25 September 1997. The decision was published in the book, The Case for the Realisation of the Property of the Lands of the United States of America, Volume 1, published by P.O.W. Press, Inc. (P.J.P.I.S). The book is available in English, German, French, Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese. Costa, Mr P. Kūris, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mr W.S. Jungwiert and Mr K. Traja. The case was first heard in 1973. The applicants claimed they had not received adequate land in exchange for their land. They filed a complaint with the Administrative Court. The appeal was dismissed on 5 July 1990. The case was heard again on 25 September 1990 and the complaint was dismissed again on 5 December 1992. The application was settled out of court on 8 September 1993. The issue was decided on the basis that the land was no longer of sufficient value to be given to the applicants. The decision was not appealed on the grounds that it was not necessary to give the land to them in the first place. It was settled on the ground that they had already been given the land in question by the previous owner.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 39197/98) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court, which, on 11 September 2001, declared the application partially admissible and decided to dispense with a hearing (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The defendants applied for security for their costs, and the court granted the application on 26 September 1985 by ordering the plaintiffs to pay a sum reflecting the defendants’ likely costs up until the date for exchange of evidence. The proceedings were stayed until the security was paid. The appeal was dismissed on 31 January 1986 and the plaintiffs paid the security on 28 February 1986. The plaintiffs’ solicitors filed a Notice of Intention to Proceed on 5 January 1989 as required by the rules of court since no steps had been taken in the prosecution of the claim for more than a year. On 10 February 1989 the plaintiffs served a Summons for Directions, the deadline for which had expired on 2 February 1985. The case was referred to the High Court. The defendants made a payment into court of GBP 50,000 on 1 November 1990. The plaintiffs appealed in December 1992. The appeal was stood out of the list by consent until 31 March 1995. Ferranti Instrumentation Limited had stopped trading and ceased to exist altogether in November 1996. The applicant informed the Civil Appeals Office that he would be proceeding in person. The application for security for costs was dismissed. Mr Justice Jowitt: Is there a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias? Injustice will have occurred if “the decision-maker unfairly regarded with disfavour the case of a party to the issue under consideration by him”. The applicants expressly disavow any suggestion of actual bias. The court is not concerned strictly with the appearance of bias but rather with establishing the possibility that there was actual although unconscious bias. If there was unconscious bias on the part of the Panel, the ‘doctrine of necessity’ fell to be considered. The panel found that no unconscious bias had taken place.

Mr Justice Jowitt said there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. He concluded that, on the evidence before him, he could not say that the applicant had established that there was a real danger of injustice having occurred as a result of bias. He said: “When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty to make a decision in circumstances in which a question of bias arises, it seems to me that the court must necessarily be asking itself whether there is areal danger that the decision-maker was unconsciously biased” (9) It is not necessary for the applicant to demonstrate a real possibility that the ... decision would have been different but for the bias, he said.

Mr Justice Jowitt: A real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability. It is not necessary for the applicant to demonstrate a real possibility that the ... decision would have been different but for the bias. What must be established is the real danger of bias having affected the decision in the sense of having caused the decision-maker, albeit unconsciously, to weigh the competing contentions, and so decide the merits, unfairly. He concluded that there was no unconscious bias on the part of any of the Panel members. He said: “When a body is charged by statute with the power or duty, which cannot be delegated, to make a decision in circumstances in which a question of bias arises, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered”

The Court of Appeal refused an application for leave to appeal from Mr Justice Jowitt's decision. Lord Justice Morritt (with whom Lord Justice Hobhouse agreed) held, on the “doctrine of necessity,” as follows: “I am prepared to assume in favour of [the applicant] that he would have an arguade against the Panel’s decision”. The applicant failed to establish that the Panel's decision was irrational or unreasonable or to make out any sufficient ground for judicial review. The decision will not be liable to be impugned on account of bias provided that: (i) if only some of those charged with the power or duty to decide are potentially affected by bias such of them as can lawfully withdraw do so; and (ii) those of the decision-makers who are potentially involved use their best endeavours to avoid the effect of bias.

Mr Justice Jowitt said there was a real risk that the decision of the tribunal had been actuated by bias. I am bound to say that, on that limited point, I think he was manifestly right. The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. On 14 September 1999 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section (“the Chamber”). The case was decided in favour of the application on the grounds that the hearing had never taken place and that it should not have been held. The first judgment dealt with the applicant's appeal. The decision was challenged on the grounds that the Panel was biased, or had the appearance of bias, and that its findings were vitiated by errors of law and were irrational. The appeal was dismissed in January 1996 after the judge delivered three separate judgments. Mr Justice Jowitt dealt with “Wednesbury’ challenges to the findings in respect of the various complaints made of him. He found that the Board's conclusion – that what took place amounted to an agreement between Mr S. and LCL, such that section 16 was breached – was a conclusion it was entitled to reach. The judge described the test of bias under English law in the following terms (pp. 93-96 of the judgment): “[Counsel for the applicant] submits that the decision to revoke the applicant's section 19 certificates of approval should be quashed because the Panel was biased” An applicant has first to show from the evidence that there is an appearance of bias. He then has to go on to show that on a proper examination by the court of the evidence before it there is demonstrated a real danger of injustice. By “real” is meant not without substance. A real danger clearly involves more than a minimal risk, less than a probability. A decision-maker may have unfairly regarded with disfavour one party's case either consciously or unconsciously. He stated that if, contrary to his finding, there was unconscious bias on the part of the Panel, the “doctrine of necessity” fell to be considered. Counsel for the applicant submitted that the Board had failed to take the reasonable steps to minimise the risk of bias affecting them. The judge said that the decision of the Board was not liable to be impugned on account of bias provided that: (i) if only some of those charged with the power or duty to decide are potentially affected by bias such of them as can lawfully withdraw from the decision-making do so. Mr Justice Jowitt rejected the submission, on the grounds that no useful reference could have been made to an independent tribunal which did not involve an impermissible delegation. The applicant failed to establish that the Panel's decision was irrational or unreasonable or to make out any sufficient ground for judicial review. Lord Justice Morritt (with whom Lord Justice Hobhouse agreed) held that there was a real risk that the decision of the tribunal had been actuated by bias even though they were not in fact biased against him. The decision for the Board was, at the end of the day, whether or not Mr Kingsley was a fit and proper person. "There is no meaningful independent panel and the decision would stand because the decision has to be made by the Board and could not be delegated to the independent tribunal," he adds. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). Informant told police that the applicant had been involved in the murder of David Beesley. Detective Chief Inspector Dunn requested permission for the cell and the visiting areas used by the applicant and Leroy Grant to be bugged with audio and video technology. In the interviews with the police which followed, the police told the applicant that he was not obliged to say anything. He availed himself of that right. The applicant was invited to comment on the recordings made in February and March 1995. He made no comment to any question. According to the applicant, he was interrogated. After 20 April 1995 he associated regularly with the applicant who was remanded at Strangeways Prison. eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. The decision was made in favour of the applicant, who lives in Esbjerg. The Danish Embassy in Nairobi was contacted by the applicant on 9 August 2005. She had been living in Kenya with her father’s friends while taking care of her grandmother. The Immigration Service found that her residence permit had lapsed because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. She was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act, since the applicant was 17 years old and the said provision only extended a right to family reunification to children below the age of 15. Finally, it found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permit. On 1 October 2007 the Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. The Ministry emphasises that there is no information available of any circumstances that would lead to [the applicant’s] residence permit being deemed not to have lapsed. The Immigration Service received a questionnaire from the applicant dated 12 July 2007 used for requests for exemption from the authorities revoking a residence permit despite a stay outside Denmark for a certain period. It was partly filled out and stated, inter alia, that the applicant spoke Danish, but could not read or write the language. Immigration Service brought the case concerning section 17 and section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act before the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret), before which the case was decided on the documents submitted. On 25 April 2008 it found against the applicant. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret), henceforth the applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. It is stated for the record that it was not [the applicant's] decision to leave Denmark and stay away so long. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention. The applicant's parents sent her voluntarily to Kenya to live with family for an indefinite period. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien’s Act and the possibility of submitting an application for asylum under section 7 of the Aliens Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The High Court upheld the City Court's decision to refuse the applicant a residence permit on 30 October 2008. It took into account that the applicant was seventeen years and nine months old, when in August 2005 she applied to re-enter Denmark.

It originated in an application (no. 10300/83) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mrs. Martha Nölkenbockhoff, on 7 February 1983. The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber. The Government, the Commission and the applicant appeared before the Court. The Court heard addresses by Mrs. Maier for the Government and by Mr. Weitzel for the Commission, as well as their replies to its questions. On 29 November, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court (Rule 50). The hearing was held in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. The case is now before the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which will rule on the case at the end of the year. If you would like to make a donation to the ECHR, please visit www.echr.org.uk. Martha Nölkenbockhoff is the widow and heir of Mr. Theodor Nönkenbocks. Her husband was a senior manager in a holding company, Stumm AG. He was found guilty of breach of trust (Untreue), criminal bankruptcy (Bankrott) and fraud (Betrug) and given an aggregate sentence of eight years' imprisonment. His four co-defendants were also sentenced to prison terms - two of them, for more or less identical offences and a few additional ones, to nine years, nine months and to eight years, six months respectively. In respect of a series of fraud charges, the Regional Court stayed the proceedings under Article 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 23 below) Mr. Nölkenbockhoff entered an appeal on points of law on the same day that judgment was given. The Federal Court of Justice (Bundesgerichtshof) had not given a decision by the time he died on 13 November. Three of the co-defendants, who had likewise challenged the Regional Court’s judgment, later withdrew their appeals. The appeal lodged by the fourth person convicted, Mr. M, was dismissed by the Federal Court on 7 July 1982 as being manifestly ill-founded. The applicant sought orders that the Treasury should bear the necessary costs and expenses incurred by her late husband in connection with his conviction. On 5 March 1982, the Essen Regional Court found against Mrs. Nölkenbockhoff. She requested the Regional Court to adjourn a decision on her applications until such time as the Federal Court of Justice had given judgment on the appeal brought by the co-defendant Mr. M. The applications are admissible ... but ill-founded. Where proceedings are terminated by reason of a defendant’s death, his necessary costs and expenses are normally borne by the Treasury, but this does not apply where, were it not for this technical bar, the defendant would almost certainly have been convicted. This was so in the instant case. The court declines to award compensation for the time spent in detention on remand. The reasons given for the judgment are not consistent with its assessment of the case as a whole. The court does not consider it necessary to defer judgment until a decision has been given on the co-defendant M’s appeal on points of law. The applicant appealed to the Hamm Court of Appeal against that decision on 11 March 1982. In written pleadings dated 18 March, she challenged, inter alia, the Regional Court's finding that, had her husband not died, he “would almost certainly have been convicted or his conviction almost certainly would have been upheld’. It was as if it were sought to obtain a final (abschliessend) conviction of the deceased by a side wind in the form of a decision as to costs. The Regional Court likewise disregarded the presumption of innocence in stating that the grounds of appeal afforded no reason to suppose that the defendant would have been acquitted. The court should have known that vital points in Mr. Nölkenbockhoff’s appeal were also relied on by the co-defendant M. The applicant pointed out in addition that from the outset her husband had denied having committed any offences and had indeed been acquitted on several counts. Since criminal law was based on the principle of individual guilt, it was quite simply unacceptable - and, once again, contrary to Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2) - to judge the deceased. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Supreme Court's decision not to recognise his right to succeed to a tenancy after the death of his companion amounted to discrimination on the ground of his sexual orientation. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court. By a decision of 11 September 2001 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 7 December 2001 the President of the Chamber granted ILGA-Europe (The European Region of the International Lesbian and Gay Association) leave to intervene as third parties.

The applicant attended Dunderrow National School from 1968. The school was owned, through trustees, by the Catholic Bishop of the Diocese of Cork and Ross. The Irish Human Rights Commission and the European Centre for Law and Justice had been given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure. In 1996 she was contacted by the police who were investigating a complaint made in 1995 by a former pupil of Dunderrow National School against L. h. The judge decided that the allegations were not substantiated and that the prosecution of L. H. were likely to be successful. Dissenting churches and the Catholic Church wished to ensure that children of their denominations be educated in schools controlled by the denomination and not by the State. Hardiman J went on to describe as ‘remarkable’ the fact that, whilst in nineteenth-century Europe firmer distinctions were being drawn between Church and State. He noted that, in recent times and after more than a century and a half, the provision of education was belatedly and at least partially placed on a statutory basis by the Education Act 1998. He was unaware that a CCTV camera, mounted on the traffic island in front of the junction, filmed his movements. The CCTV footage later disclosed did not show the applicant cutting his wrists. The operator was solely alerted to an individual in possession of a knife at the junctions. The police were notified by the CCTV operator and arrived. They took the knife from the applicant, gave him medical assistance and brought him to the police station. The applicant became aware that he had been filmed on CCTV and that footage had been released because a neighbour told his partner that the former had seen him on television. Anglia Television sought, and the Council provided, footage of the incident involving the applicant. On 17 October 1995 extracts from that footage were included in its news programme about the CCTV system, a local broadcast to an average audience of 350,000. The applicant's face had been masked at the Council's oral request. However, that masking was later considered inadequate by the Independent Television Commission (see below), the applicant's distinctive hairstyle and moustache making him easily recognisable to anyone who knew him. A letter of 25 April 1996 from the Yellow Advertiser opined that the applicant was not identifiable. The BBC agreed to use the footage if it did not identify the person. The request was denied by the BBC. The man was identified when the footage was shown on national television. He also appeared on the BBC radio programme ‘Right to Listen’. He was never identified in the final broadcast of ‘Crime Beat’ in May 1996. The footage was never used in any further broadcast of the programme. The BBC has not apologised for the use of the man’s image on the programme or for the decision to remove the mask from the footage in the first place. The original request for the footage from the BBC was refused. The Council has not issued an apology. The applicant lodged a complaint with the BSC in relation to, inter alia, the “Crime Beat” programme alleging an unwarranted infringement of his privacy. He also had his photograph published in the Yellow Advertiser on 25 October 1996. The BSC upheld both of his complaints on 13 June 1997. The BBC was directed to broadcast a summary of the adjudication with the episode of ‘Crime Beat' on 12 June 1997 and a summary in The Daily Telegraph on 12 July 1997. It found that the applicant's identity was not adequately obscured and that he was readily identifiable and easily recognisable by those who knew him. The ITC found that section 2(2) and (5) of the Code had been breached. The applicant complained to the PCC in respect of the articles published in the Yellow Advertiser. The PCC rejected the applicant's complaint without a hearing and the decision was communicated to the applicant by letter dated 2 August 1996. The applicant applied to the High Court for leave to apply for judicial review of the Council's disclosure of the CCTV material arguing, inter alia, that that disclosure had no basis in law. On 26 June 1996 a single judge of the High court refused leave. The High Court granted leave on a renewed request and leave to amend the application to include a complaint that the disclosure was irrational, even if lawful. The High Court judge had some sympathy with that submission but did not consider it correct in law. He argued that by failing to consult the police to see if he had been charged with a criminal offence and to impose sufficient restrictions as regards disclosure of his identity, the Council had facilitated an unwarranted invasion of his privacy. Unless and until there is a general right of privacy recognised by English law, reliance must be placed on effective guidance being issued by Codes of practice or otherwise, said the judge. In the case, the film footage showed a man walking in the High Street carrying a large knife in his hand. It did not show him attempting to commit suicide. Anglia TV failed to mask the applicant's identity adequately. The BBC failed to disguise the applicant at all in the trailers. Brentwood Borough Council were notified about that by the applicant. The Council immediately contacted the BBC and received assurances that his image had been masked. In the event, unknown to the Council, it had not been adequately masked in the programme. I am sure that lessons can be learnt from this unfortunate incident, and it may be that, with the benefit of hindsight, the Council will want to see if they can tighten up their guidelines to seek to avoid a similar incident in the future.” An application to the High Court for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal was rejected.

The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Sussex. His wife died on 29 October 2000 and he had no children from the marriage. His claim for widows’ benefits was made on 2 January 2001 and was rejected on 31 May 2001. The applicant did not appeal as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under United Kingdom law. I. The circumstances of the case are as follows: The applicant’s wife died in October 2000. He was not entitled to widows' benefits because he was not a woman. He is entitled to such benefits as he is a widower under UK law.
